speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure to authorize the Canadian National Railway Company to issue securities not exceeding $29,414,206 in principal amount to provide the moneys necessary to meet capital expenditures made or capital indebtedness incurred during the calendar year 1941; to make provision for the purchase or refunding of capital obligations of the company or of any company comprised in the Canadian National Railways system and for the issue of substituted securities for such purposes; to authorize the governor in council to guarantee the principal, interest and sinking funds of securities issued by the company for the purposes aforesaid; to authorize the making of temporary loans to the said company secured by such securities and not exceeding $29,414,206 in principal amount to enable the said company to meet such expenditures and indebtedness; with authority to give financial aid and assistance to other companies of the said national system; to authorize the company to pay supplementary contributions to

C.N.R.-Guarantee oj Securities
certain railway employees' provident funds; and to authorize the making of further temporary loans to the said company for interim deficits, said loans to be reimbursed from the annual revenues.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Vien in the chair.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
I ask the minister to make a general statement covering the necessity of this measure. I am aware that this is the usual resolution preceding the introduction of a bill. Certain portions of the resolution are obviously necessary, having regard to the operations of the railways, such as authorizing the company to make supplementary contributions to the employees' provident funds, the giving of temporary loans, and that sort of thing. But I should like the minister to give, for the purposes of the record, a break-down of the twenty-nine odd millions, and to explain why, with the revenues of the railway mounting beyond any previous levels-having regard, of course, to the great increase of traffic which is largely if not wholly due to the war-there is no indication on the part of the management that this year an operating surplus may be expected, which might be devoted to purposes other than, we will say, working capital. I am astonished that there is no suggestion of an operating profit this year. I am astonished, having regard to the growth of traffic, that last year we had to provide in the neighbourhood of 817,000,000. I am afraid that there is not the economy visible in the operation of the system that there ought to be. I am making no attack on the railway. I believe that the national railways are doing excellent work in connection with the country's war operations. In the eastern provinces, at all events, they are moving a very great amount of traffic. But the country is paying them at the approved rates for all this traffic, and they mukt be in receipt of very substantial sums of money from the war appropriation fund- millions in excess of what anybody knows about.
The railways are embarking on capital expenditures of a character which seem to me to be unnecessary at the moment. No great system of railways, indeed no business, can be carried on without annual capital expenditures. They cannot be static; they must go forward. But I wonder if the government has given consent to certain capital expenditures which have already been undertaken. I have in mind the installation of the electric control between Pacific Junction and Truro, which will cost at least one and a half million dollars and will probably run to two millions, involving also the expenditure of at least half
a million dollars of United States exchange at a time when there is need to conserve our exchange position, and that in respect to a project which must be regarded as somewhat of an experiment in a cold climate such as that of Canada.
Frankly, when I heard about this I wrote to one of the vice-presidents and received in confidence from him a statement of the railway position. I am bound to say that he made what was to me a convincing statement of the utility of the proposal. But there is in this country a view that at this time the government should not permit the railway company to embark upon expenditures of this kind, which can be justified only because of the war. And how many crimes are committed in that name? When the war is over this expenditure will be useless, I am informed. I believe it operates with great advantage in the winter time in countries which have not the severe weather conditions that we have in Canada, The idea is of course to relieve congestion. It is an electrical mechanical device intended to supersede employment on the railway itself. I am convinced that the proposal has its merits, but I want to know what is the justification at this time for this capital expenditure, having regard to the fact that it constitutes a substantial charge on the foreign exchange control position and on the conservation of our exchange.
I would ask the minister to give the house a statement with regard to the Montreal terminal, which is not yet completed and which will cost about $30,000,000, a very considerable portion of which was expended in war time. In no sense can this work be justified as a war measure, and it involves millions in foreign exchange. I should like the minister to give the house information with respect to what is being done in connection with the redemption of equipment trust certificates. This is an old problem in connection with the national railways. There is in effect what is commonly called the Philadelphia plan, whereby railways acquire rolling stock on the basis of deferred payments. As a rule the railways make an initial payment. The equipment is mortgaged under trust agreement to a trustee, who issues securities and the money is payable in a term of years, or from year to year in serial form. It was looked upon with great favour by investors in days gone by, but as regards the Canadian National Railways, especially in the darker days when the earnings were not sufficient, these equipment trust payments, if my memory serves me rightly, were not made out of earnings at all but out of sums advanced by the government against which long-term

C.N.R.-Guarantee oj Securities
securities were eventually issued, constituting in turn a dead-weight debt on the system, and covering in some instances a period expiring at a date beyond the lifetime of the equipment.
I should like to know how much of this $29,000,000 is in payment of equipment trust certificates issued and maturing, which the company is not able to take up out of operating expenses, which is the basis of the whole plan. I should be happy if the minister could assure me that none of this $29,000,000 is to be devoted to that purpose, though I know from past experience that substantial portions of capital authorizations have had to be so used because the railways did not have the moneys to retire these obligations. If the minister is able to assure the house and the country that in this connection the railway is taking care of its commitments and that no new securities will be issued against these payments, no long-term securities which the railway cannot absorb, it will be a matter of relief to all of us.
The particular point to which I desire to call the attention of the minister is the one I adverted to earlier in my remarks. Will he explain to the house why, with greatly increased traffic earnings, there is no budget before us looking to a credit balance in operations this year. It may be that my understanding is incorrect, but the country will expect that the system this year will take care of its operating expenses, interest on sinking fund charges and maturities falling due for equipment trust payments. But over and above that, with the revenues mounting, as I know they are, as we see in the press weekly, to heights hitherto unthought of or unheard of, I do not understand why there should not be a substantial credit balance to the treasury of the railway company, which in turn would be reflected in the operations of the Canadian treasury, to take care of some of the deficits of the past year or to reach such other destination as may be suggested. Or is it the theory of the railway company that it will not disclose to the house and country just what its actual expectations are, so that it may have in hand a substantial sum of money which it may use to embark on other enterprises, which parliament will not know anything about but of which of course, if they are capital, the ministry will know, and to which both the ministry and finally parliament will have to give consent on an ex post facto basis. That is what is happening. Expenditures are being incurred on capital account and all that parliament is called upon to do is to ratify what the management does.

I am not questioning the judgment of the management in most cases. Probably if left alone and freed from political interference the management would operate the road on a basis that would show returns, especially when the earning power is as high as it is to-day. But every once in a while some minister, like the Minister of Transport, steps into the picture and says, "You have to honour my election pledges." That is exactly what has happened in connection with the Montreal terminal. It is a shocking thing. I have said it on more than one occasion, and I repeat it here to-day: this country was called upon to pay an election debt of $30,000,000 because the Minister of Transport, then the Minister of Public Works, made an election pledge in a by-election in Montreal years before the war began. However desirable it was to clear up the railway situation existing in Montreal it is little less than criminal to keep on with the work when the country is spending at the rate of $5,000,000 a day on the war effort. We are being taxed to the limit to pay for this war, yet the country is asked to meet a $30,000,000 capital expenditure to fill up that hole in the ground in Montreal in order to redeem the word of the Minister of Transport, then the Minister of Public Works.
There are many other things that I could refer to, but generally speaking I want to know why it was that with all the traffic that accrued to the system, splendid increases during the last year, it went behind $17,000,000, and this year is budgeting for no profit on operations. It is incomprehensible to me. Every class one railroad on the north American continent is doing better. The United States has not yet entered the war but is approximating that position, and as a result there has been a great increase in railway traffic. Every railway in the United States is budgeting for increased earnings, in most cases sufficiently large to take them out of the red. I have in mind at the moment the New Haven system, which operates in New England. A very large portion of their revenue comes from passenger traffic, which has felt bus competition perhaps even in a greater degree than freight traffic has felt truck competition. Yet I saw the statement very recently that the New Haven is budgeting for a surplus on operations next year.
I am delighted to see that earnings are going up by leaps and bounds, because as long as that state of things continues it makes more remote the time when we shall be called upon again-if we ever are; I hope we never shall be-to pay operating deficits. But the minister and the management should explain why it

C.N.R.-Guarantee oj Securities
was that we had to pay an operating deficit last year of $17,000,000, in addition as I understand-I am subject to correction-to arrangements for new capital expenditure; and why it is that they are budgeting for no profit this year. This information is due to the Canadian people and I would ask the minister to give us the fullest possible statement.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
The hon. leader of the
opposition should not forget that a considerable amount of money has been already spent on the terminal station at Montreal. The plan was made a long time ago, but on account of the depression the work was suspended for some time. The money that has been spent is an investment and an asset, but it is a dead asset so long as the work is not completed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
I should
like to have the defence come from the minister, not the hon. member for Temiscouata.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
But as a member from
the province of Quebec I can say a few words before the minister answers. I am not answering in place of the minister. As a member from the province of Quebec I am answering complaints made by the leader of the opposition about expenditures made in the province of Quebec.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
I was
not complaining because the expenditure is made in the province of Quebec. The hon. member for Temiscouata must not try to represent me as an enemy of Quebec or of the national system. I object to that. It is not the basis of my remarks, although I have no doubt that will be the basis of his remarks in the province of Quebec.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
I do not say that, and the leader of the opposition, like any other hon. member, should obey the rules. I have the floor. I did not utter the words that the leader of the opposition has imputed to me, and it is just as bad to put words in the mouth of a member who has not uttered them as to impute motives. Besides, although the hon. member for York-Sunbury is the leader of the opposition, be has no more rights than the member for Temiscouata or the member for any other constituency. Therefore when I have the floor I object strongly to the leader of the opposition rising as he did, unless he rises to a question of privilege or asks permission to interrupt me. I give him that little lesson in parliamentary practice; it may be useful to him. I do not want to be interrupted by him any more, and I do not want him to put words in my mouth that I have not uttered. He is a little older
than I am and it is time he read the rules. He has enough experience to be able to understand them.
That being said, I never stated that the leader of the opposition was an enemy of the province of Quebec. What I said was that it is because this money is being spent in Montreal that there is so much criticism.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Nobecause it is war time.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
No; it was undertaken before the war, and it is important to complete it now. When my hon. friend comes from his beautiful country into the city of Montreal he does not come into a station, he comes into a shed. The most shameful so-called station in Canada is that of the Canadian National Railways in Montreal. Every hon. member who has visited the metropolis of Canada knows that. It is filthy, it is abominable, it is a bad advertisement for Canada. I believe that the government was very wise not ;to spend at once the whole amount required for the construction of that station. It was done gradually as conditions permitted. But it was rightly done, and now there is a small amount, something like $2,000,000, required to complete it and make the dead asset a live* asset. Surely that is worth doing. It is very good business. My hon. friend must remember that at the time Mr. Bennett was in power

I do not know whether he was then a minister, but at any rate he was a member supporting that government-the big sign that faces up Windsor street in Montreal beside the Bonaventure station, the sign that is seen from the Windsor hotel, was not lighted for months and months, and it was only as a result of protests of Liberal members that it was lighted again. It was the Canadian Pacific Railway company that asked the government not to light it, because it was too good an advertisement for the national railways. That is the kind of petty thing that was done by the Bennett government for the Canadian Pacific railway and against the Canadian National railways.
Where does this protest come from? It comes from the Canadian Pacific railway. Either knowingly or not the hon. gentleman is arguing the case of the C.P.R. against the C.N.R. when he complains about the construction of the new terminal in Montreal. Montreal is a growing city. Montreal is much larger now than it was when the terminal was started, and the hon. gentleman has travelled enough to see that in many places the big railways have stations that are rather close together. But I would ask the hon. gentleman another question. Let him speak about the closing of the Canadian
C.N.R.-Guarantee of Securities

National station in his own beautiful city of Fredericton. After I am through I should like him 'to give some explanation about that. Fredericton is not as large as Montreal, but it is the capital city of the great province of New Brunswick and I do not understand why the Canadian National station there should be closed. When was it closed? And was it not the hon. gentleman himself who asked to have the Canadian National Station closed at Fredericton?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: The hon. gentleman does me too much honour.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
Just a moment; my hon. friend will have an opportunity to speak when I am through. One spring there was so much ice in the river that the bridge at Fredericton was carried away; and it was due to the persistent effort and very excellent work of the hon. gentleman's illustrious predecessor, Hon. W. G. Clark, now lieutenant governor of New Brunswick and then one -of my best aides on the civil service committee, that the bridge was rebuilt. I am sure the hon. gentleman will not say that was a useless expenditure; I am sure he will not make any joking references to war-time expenditures in reference to the Fredericton bridge. But-1 wonder if it would have been rebuilt'if the Bennett government had been in power, and the hon. gentleman had been a member of that government. I know the trouble that was experienced by the great lieutenant governor of the great province of New Brunswick in having that bridge constructed; he did very excellent work, and he was successful. We did not complain about it; we realized that it was necessary and in the public interest.
The hon. gentleman is so much concerned about the importance of his functions that he does not like an ordinary hon. member to speak to him; he wants to be answered only by a minister of the crown. A privy councillor can be answered only by a minister, he believes; a back bencher, or a member of the rank and file, has not the right to answer the hon. gentleman. Well, I am not impressed by high hats. When I was a child I was told that a cat might look at a queen, I am not a cat; the hon. gentleman is not a queen; all comparisons are odious, but everyone will understand what I mean. I want the hon. gentleman to be just as generous to Montreal as Quebec members have been to Fredericton and Toronto, the holy city. We do not complain about anything when it is useful and necessary. Let' us not be narrow; let us not be pettifogging; let us not be hair-splitters, and in our humble spheres let us all try to be builders of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
The first criticism offered by the leader of the opposition had to do with the absence of a prospective surplus in the finances of the Canadian National for the year 1941. I am afraid the hon. gentleman is asking a little too much. The situation of the Canadian National is most encouraging, however, from the financial point of view; and if there is no indication of a surplus in dollars and cents for 1941 at least we have the pleasure of observing that this year parliament is not called upon to provide for any deficit, as we have had to do in the years gone by. The position of the railway this year is going to be better by at least sixteen or seventeen million dollars, and it is because the revenues of the Canadian National have increased that we are able to avoid the necessity of coming to parliament to make up the annual deficit.
My hon. friend made one observation which I aim quite sure did not come from his heart. He indicated, or rather insinuated, that the present directors of the Canadian National were not as free in their deliberations and the exercise of their judgment as they have been in the past. I can assure my hon. friend that nothing has been done to interfere with the free disposition of Canadian National affairs by the Canadian National board of directors. I have not interfered in any manner with the exercise of their judgment; I have not pressed my views upon them contrary to their will or against the public interest.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
What
about your predecessor?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
I imagine I could say the same thing about my predecessors, but I would not like to go into that field because I might be inclined to say things as to which I have some information but about which I am not perfectly sure. At all events let me reassure my hon. friend that the board of directors is as free now as it has ever been since the inception of the Canadian National system.
The hon. gentleman referred to two capital expenditures which apparently he does not like. The first was the expenditure to be made in the establishment of a central traffic control between Pacific Junction and Truro.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: I did not say I did not like it; I questioned the advisability of that expenditure in war time, and wondered whether the system would be efficacious in our climate.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: This recommendation came directly from the management of the Canadian National.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
I have no doubt about that.

354i
C.N.R.-Guarantee of Securities

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: The expenditure is being made on the basis of a strong recommendation coming from the technical officers of the Canadian National. I had no knowledge, and the government had no knowledge, of this matter before it was suggested to us in a report made by the officials of the railway, and the reason for it is the increase in traffic which has developed, more particularly since the beginning of the war.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: I accept that without reservation.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: My hon. friend knows the situation exactly in that locality. The directors of the Canadian National admit that they might be able to 'handle the situation that exists at present in that section of the line; but with the traffic continually increasing, and having in mind representations of the Department of Munitions and Supply and other war organizations that during 1941 and 1942 the railway will have to look after much more traffic, they are afraid that a bottle-neck may develop in that section;, which is mainly a single track service.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: And a one way service.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Yes; and it is the, opinion of the technical men and officials of the company that otherwise it would be impossible properly and satisfactorily to handle a much heavier traffic over that line.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Will the minister say whether at any time, because of congestion in the winter season, which I admit, the transportation of goods for overseas has been delayed? In other words will he say that a single ship has been forced to stay at an eastern Canadian port for lack of cargo?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: No, I cannot say that; my hon. friend is quite correct. Up to the present time the railway facilities have been adequate to meet the situation, and as a matter of fact the Canadian National has taken more traffic to Halifax than the port has been capable of handling.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
I think
that is true.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: But the port facilities of Halifax are being developed, and that development will increase tremendously during 1941. A proposal has been advanced to use a certain number of lighters, on which the freight will be transferred from the railroad cars to the ships in the port.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: They are going to adopt a lighterage system?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Yes, and the facilities at the port of Halifax are to be substantially developed. According to information we get from the officials of the Canadian National Railways there is not only the possibility but the probability that with the present railway facilities between Pacific Junction and Truro we would not be able to handle the traffic.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
Would the
alternative be a double track?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
That would be more
expensive.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
Yes, I
believe so.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: In all sincerity I can assure my hon. friend that the directors and technical men of the Canadian National Railways were in no shape or form influenced by the minister or by the government in proposing such an expenditure.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: I am prepared to accept that.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
They thought it was in the best interests of the Canadian National Railways, and believed it to be absolutely necessary in order to avoid the creation of what is known as a bottle-neck in that section of our line.
I come now to another point with which my name has been often associated. On many occasions in different parts of the country and in the House of Commons it has been suggested that I forced the hand of the Canadian National Railways toward the completion of the Montreal terminal. That is not the situation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
Perhaps
that is a crude way of putting it.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
What I said in Montreal, and what I advocated not only on one but on several occasions, was only the adoption of a proposal which had come from the railway itself. The completion of the Montreal terminal is not being imposed upon the Canadian National Railways by the present minister or the government, either now or at any time. I advocated the completion of the terminal because the technical advisers and officials of the railway had expressed the view that it was desirable and in its interest that it be completed. One has but to remember what the situation was, in order' to realize the truth of that suggestion. Many people have a misconception of the whole situation. The terminal project was originated as far back as 1929, when the revenues of the railways were increasing substantially. Work was

C.N.R.-Guarantee of Securities
abandoned in 1931 or 1932, when we reached the depression years. But when the question was revived in 1939 the Canadian people had already invested in that terminal nearly $17,000,000. It was lying as a dead asset; it was bringing in no revenue, giving no facilities to the railway, in a word remaining in the same position as that in which it has stood for a long time.
It was decided in 1939 to proceed further with the work. I might add in passing that I had no responsibility with respect to railways at that time. The scheme was one which first of all involved an exenditure of $53,000,000 or $55,000,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: A grandiloquent scheme.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
Yes. It was reexamined in 1939, and it was then established that with an additional expenditure of about $12,000,000 the work would be completed and facilities made available. It was thought at that time it would be in the interests of the Canadian National Railways to take advantage of the large expenditure which had been made up to that date, but which was then lying dormant, and to proceed with the work. The question has been before the committee on railways and shipping. It has been approved by a majority of the representatives of the people of Canada. It has been discussed and examined in all its aspects by members of the committee, and has been discussed openly in parliament.
When I spoke in Montreal-and I am not ashamed of what I said; I do not wish to retract one word-I only expressed the desire and indicated my determination to see that a project which had been proposed by the railway itself should be carried out. Any man who has knowledge of the city of Montreal, and of the facilities in that city at the disposal of the Canadian National Railways, will not hesitate to admit that something must be done at that point, if the Canadian National railway system is to expect to obtain its fair share of the traffic in freight and passengers. It is entitled to that traffic.
Any citizen of Canada, whether he lives in Montreal, Winnipeg or Vancouver, can be proud of and satisfied with work which will do away with that rat-nest which is called Bonaventure station in Montreal, and no people, except citizens of Montreal, would have tolerated such a condition so long.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
And a
war on! We are always being told there is a war on.
[Mr. Cardin.J

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
They are the only people
in Canada who have been tolerating a situation such as the one which has existed in Montreal since 1929. In 1939, $17,000,000 had already been expended, and to make the terminal useful there was involved the matter of adding $12,000,000 in order to complete the project and to make it a useful and profitable undertaking for the railway.
People are arguing as though the government were spending $30,000,000 this year on the Montreal terminal. We see articles in the newspapers and listen to speeches in which the question is asked: "What is the use of spending $30,000,000 to provide a terminal in Montreal?" That is not the situation at all. Those who speak that way simply desire to prejudice public opinion outside this house against the interests of the Canadian National Railways. I have explained that $17,000,000 had been spent before the work was stopped in 1931. Since 1939, when the project was revived, there will have been spent

including this year's expenditures-the sum of $12,000,000, to revive that project and to turn it into a reasonable and profitable undertaking for the railway.
This matter involves not only the building of a station. The Montreal terminal project covers the relaying of tracks and the opening of the coach yard at Point St. Charles, the unifying of five Canadian National railway stations, and does away with twenty level crossings in St. Henri, a very active centre of Montreal. What has been done? Up to the present we have disposed of eleven of those level crossings, which had been responsible for the deaths of many people and had caused enormous delays in the handling of freight and passenger trains, to the detriment of the Canadian National Railways.
If the project is completed, the remaining nine of the twenty level street crossings will be relieved to a large extent, because passenger traffic will be taken off them. Only the freight traffic to be handled at the Bonaventure and Turcot terminals will remain. When the new station is established the passenger, mail and express traffic will pass through the new station, and the Bonaventure and Turcot areas will be used only for the transportation of freight. This will give freight handling facilities to the railway covering an area of
21,000	square feet of space at present occupied by express and mail services in Bonaventure station. Instead of moving passenger coaches several miles from Bonaventure station to Turcot station, they will be moved to the new coach yard which has been established at Point St. Charles.

C.N.R.-Guarantee of Securities
Many people seem to have a misconception of the situation and express exaggerated views. Their minds have been affected to a certain extent by propaganda which has been put out, not in this house, against the Canadian National Railways and in favour of its competitor. I am not afraid to mention it; that is the situation. As a member of the government, as one having something to do with the Canadian National Railways, as a citizen of Canada, I want to give this organization of the people a fair opportunity of competing with its principal competitor and others in the handling of freight and passengers. It is of no use to complain that the Canadian National Railways is not doing this or that, is not up to standard. Let us give to the Canadian National Railways the necessary facilities to fight their own battles-as Mr. Churchill has said "give them the tools"- and they will be in position to show better results than they have shown in the past. Probably in the counse of a year or two they will be able to show what my hon. friends 'have been asking for, a surplus, which will help to reduce the indebtedness of the country in regard to this great undertaking.
I have no desire to hurt the Canadian Pacific Railway. I have the greatest respect and consideration for that company, and have always admired the men who have directed its affairs. At all times I have been proud as a Canadian of the developments which have resulted from the establishment of the Canadian Pacific Railway. But conditions have been such that the Canadian people now own a railway system which has been acquired with their own money. It is only right that we should give it a fair deal and provide it with all the reasonable facilities it requires for thg proper handling of freight and passengers and the betterment of its position.
Without wanting to be unfair or to hurt the feelings of anyone, which is not my practice, I must say I was surprised at the attitude taken by certain hon. gentlemen in regard to the Canadian National Railways. To a large extent the Canadian National Railways is the baby of hon. gentlemen opposite. It was in 1917, under the war measures act of that day and under closure, that the Canadian Northern Railway became the property of the Canadian people. A price of 810,000,000 was paid for the shares of a railway which was in such financial condition that it had to be purchased in order to preserve the service. It was during a war that that expenditure was made, and I think I have some reason for saying that to a certain extent it is the child of most of those who criticize the Canadian National Railways to-day. Apparently they are blaming us
because we are not ready to strangle their own baby, because we want to provide for its growing up, because we want it to be able to take a proper place in the affairs of the country. That is the situation. The Liberal party is not responsible for it. We accepted the gift when we came into power in 1921; we undertook the task. I can recall the speeches that were delivered then.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Does the minister not remember the attitude taken by the then member for La Prairie-Napierville, who sat about where the minister now sits, and who said that he was going to give it away for a dollar?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
I remember that. I
remember quite well when the question was raised in the House of Commons in 1917. I was in the house at the time and I remember the bitter discussion that took place between the present leader of the Conservative party in the other house, and the Right Hon. Mr. Bennett. Those two gentlemen were not in agreement. In those days Mr. Meighen was advocating the purchase of the Canadian Northern and was using all the powers of his keen intellect to convince parliament that that should be done. He even went to Montreal in order to convince St. James street that it would be a good deal to buy the Canadian Northern. He was very effective in his argument and it was a pleasure to listen to him State his case. As a back bencher I was very much interested. But he got a strong reply from Mr. Bennett, who was full of enthusiasm in those days, as he always has been. He disagreed bitterly with Mr. Meighen. Many people in Montreal and in other sections of the country did not like the decision of the so-called union government in 1917 to acquire that railway, but they accepted it. Since that time the critics have never stopped trying to interfere-I repeat, not in this house-with the free and natural development of the Canadian National Railways. They have the same interests in mind that they had when they opposed the acquisition of the Canadian Northern.
The situation is not new. The arguments which are advanced to-day, are exactly the same as those that were advanced in those days. The same arguments have always been advanced at any time that the Canadian National Railways proposed something in the way of capital expenditure in order to better its position. It is the same position, the same thing. But now they add a new dement- the war. We are all ready to admit that during the war we must dispense with certain expenditures. But that policy should

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
This afternoon at one
o'clock I was going to make a few remarks, following the minister. I listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion this morning. When the promise that the station was to be completed in Montreal, was made 
during a by-election, I felt that a great disservice had been performed to the national railways. Having said that, I am not criticizing the completion of this project, because I believe the Canadian National Railways need a terminal which is a credit to the system. Several years ago when I was travelling west by train a gentleman from the United States was sitting beside me, and in the course of the discussion I asked him if he had ever travelled across Canada on the Canadian National railway. He said, "No; my impression is that it is a rather dilapidated institution." I said, "How did you get that impression?" "Well," he said, "I have seen its station in Montreal, and I thought the railway looked like a small affair,"-on account of the station at Montreal. As a matter of fact, of course, we know that the Canadian National railway operates, at least in its transcontinental service, as fine and as comfortable and as efficient a train with as good a service as can be found anywhere in north America. I believe therefore that the completion of the terminal at Montreal is justifiable from that point of view. Unfortunately, as I have said, the announcement of the construction was injected into a by-election, with the result that many people across Canada think that the government is fulfilling a pre by-election promise. It is unfortunate that that impression should be abroad.
With regard to the resolution now before us, expenditures upon the national railway have to be made in order to provide us with the efficient transportation service which we require. I am always suspicious when the national railway is under attack, because there are people in this country who would like to see the system taken out of public hands and returned to private control. But when we look over the record we find that the competing railway, efficient and privately-owned, has probably received, taking into consideration the times in which we live, greater, or as great financial assistance as the national railway has ever received.
The Drayton-Acworth commission's report in 1917 gave some figures which, I suggest, we might well look at occasionally. It will be found that to June 30, 1916, public subsidies to private railways amounted to $163,000,000; the proceeds of land granted, $158,000,000; loans, which were never repaid, $118,000,000; guarantees of securities, over $268,000,000, and the land grants exceeded 14,700,000 acres. If we examine the record of grants to the private railway with which comparisons are so often made, we find that gifts to the Canadian Pacific Railway alone amounted to $228,500,000, plus 11,482,132 acres of land valued by

C.N.R.-Guarantee oj Securities
the company itself at over $119,000,000. Our national railway system, or those who organized it after the various bankrupt institutions were taken over by the crown, have really done a remarkable job in welding it into a strong and efficient railway system. I am not going into the history of railway building this afternoon, but it will be recalled that when the government was constructing the transcontinental railway-the Grand Trunk Pacific linked up with the section built by the government across northern Quebec and northern Ontario-the same government at the same time was guaranteeing the bonds of a third transcontinental railway which was being promoted by Mackenzie and Mann.
If one looks back at the building up of the railway, nationally owned-or rather nationally controlled, for that is the more appropriate term, since we are really operating the railway not so much for the benefit of the people of Canada as for the interests that were on the verge of bankruptcy in 1917 and 1918-1 believe that the charges which are sometimes made of extravagance-and we have an inference of extravagance at the present time-may be regarded from the point of view that, if we compare the history of the two railroads, both have been guilty of certain extravagances, and that the one has no right to cast a stone at the other.
I was looking up some figures at noon to-day, and I found, for example, that between 1923 and 1931 over $450,000,000 of capital were expended on reconditioning the run-down railways which now comprise the Canadian National railway system. In the same period of time the Canadian Pacific Railway, which was in much better shape and had far less mileage, spent $253,000,000 for the same purpose. It was a period of reconditioning and rehabilitation of railways following the great war.
I have often heard criticisms of the Canadian National system on the ground of extravagance in the building of hotels. But again let us consider the comparative expenditures. The Canadian Pacific Railway, starting with $25,000,000 invested in hotel buildings, increased the investment to $48,000,000, an addition of $23,000,000. In a similar period of time the Canadian National Railways increased their expenditures on hotels from $10,000,000 to $22,000,000, an addition of $12,000,000. Let us keep this picture clearly before us.
There are still those to-day who advocate the amalgamation of the two railway systems. I have always opposed amalgamation because I believe that the propaganda in its favour has been put out by private interests who seek the control of our transportation systems.
I believe that the national road should be retained as a national asset, and that it is our responsibility to parliament to keep it out of politics in every particular. That is why I stated at the outset that in my opinion it was unfortunate and was a grave error to inject into a by-election the building of the terminal in Montreal. It may have elected an hon. gentleman; nevertheless it has caused a great deal of criticism all across Canada. Perhaps the hon. gentleman could have been elected without that promise. I do not know.
I support the bill in so far as it will further assist our railway system to meet the needs of the time; and in the expenditure of this money to make the railway more efficient I hope the government will take into consideration the promotion in every way of the business welfare of our own government road. I have no animosity towards the privately-owned road. It has rendered a great service to the country, but it has been very well paid for that service, and I trust that our national system will continue to render a still more excellent service than it has given in the past.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
May I first of all extend my personal congratulations to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Cardin) on the vigorous manner in which he defended himself this morning. Time has not withered his intellect, whatever it may have done to his physique, and it was a pleasure to me to see him exhibit once more across the floor of this house some of that old fire which animated him in days gone by. I can safely say that as between us as individuals there has never been anything but the very best feeling, and if I made an attack upon him for the election promise he gave in the city of Montreal prior to the resuscitation of this Montreal terminal question, he will understand that I was attacking him as a politician and not as an individual.
In the course of his remarks the minister referred to .the birth of the national system. What he said in that regard was true. The system was set up by a former Conservative government on the theory, and because of the fact, that private interests had failed and that this country was at war, and that these railways could not or should not be allowed to go into the hands of a receivership at a time when the country's credit was being strained to its utmost to sustain a national war effort. That may have been a mistake; I do not know. I do not think I am in a position to judge, or that anyone is in a position to judge. At all events, that was the consensus at that time, and whether history



C.N.R.-Guarantee of Securities
has borne out the wisdom of that judgment I leave to hon. members to decide for themselves.
I do recall, however, having read with a good deal of intellectual pleasure the attacks that were made from across the floor of this house, from this place, upon the proposals then brought before parliament. If anyone wants interesting reading, I suggest that he read the speeches of D. D. McKenzie, house leader of the Liberal party when that legislation was brought into parliament. If he wants to come down to more modern times, let him read the speeches of the late Walter Mitchell in this house, delivered from that side of the house after the change of government in 1921. Let the reader see what he thought of the national railway system, and then reflect that later on the Liberal party sought to take into its bosom this orphan child which they would have condemned to death at the time of its birth.
We had better view this matter realistically. We have the national system and I think that as long as conditions are as they are to-day we shall have it. I do not want anyone to say that I am an enemy of the national system. I never have been. Personally I have consistently opposed the physical amalgamation of the two railroads. I am wondering, though, what will happen after the war. Some government may have to deal with a problem which was acute during the depression years. That is something we shall have to anticipate, and that is one reason why I want the management of the national railways at the present time to prepare for the rainy day that is bound to come, and if there is any possibility of doing so to set aside a reserve against the time which I think will come. Do not let anyone say that I have ever attacked the national system in this house. I have never had any professional connection with any railway except the national system. For ten years I acted as counsel for the system in the province of New Brunswick, between 1910 and 1921, and the former chief counsel of the railway did me the honour to say that I had won more lawsuits for the government railway system than any other counsel in any given period. I was proud of my connection with the national railways.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: They should have been proud of you.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
Well, they paid me and I think they discharged fully their obligations to me as I endeavoured to discharge my obligations to them. My remarks with respect to the management in connection with the Montreal terminals are

based upon this theory. I know that a grandiloquent scheme was started by Sir Henry Thornton, estimated to cost $60,000,000, and having regard to the expenditures that were made at that time it would probably have run into far more money than that. The undertaking was stopped, of necessity, during the depression. I know the site was an eyesore in Montreal-that "ditch" as it has been called. There were operating difficulties, but they were operating difficulties which the railway encountered and overcame for a period of more than ten years.
It was always visualized, I believe, that either the scheme itself or something analogous to it would some day be completed. It is too bad that a start was made as a result of a political promise. The minister denies that. Shall I put it this way, that the management had an intelligent anticipation of the minister's wishes. That is the moit charitable view.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: It is a great compliment the hon. member is paying me.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
I am complimentary to the minister. I have always been complimentary to him. He is of a mental and intellectual stature that commands my admiration. I dare say he is the most astute politician that ever came out of the province of Quebec. That remark is not uncomplimentary, and is not intended to be.
The resumption of this undertaking when the war broke out was astonishing. What was the government's policy with respect to all other public works? It clamped down on everything, in the interest of conservation of resources for the war effort. But this undertaking was not touched. That is what I am complaining of, and that alone. I could take hon. members down to the little city of Fredericton where an agricultural laboratory was being built. Some $7,000 was required to complete it, but the work was stopped, and unless great care has been taken the building must have greatly deteriorated. I understand arrangements were ultimately made to cover it in and save the structure. But no one has criticized that government policy. That was a proper course to pursue and is the course which ought to have been pursued in connection with the Montreal terminal. But they went on spending the money and are spending it now. Of course it would be silly to stop it at this stage and I am not suggesting that. What I was suggesting is that it could well have waited.
The hon. member for Temiscouata did me too much honour in suggesting that I was the instigator or father of the idea of union

C.N.R.-Guarantee oj Securities
terminals in Fredericton. What was the position there? Both railways enter that city; each had separate freight facilities and separate passenger facilities. The freight facilities of the national railway were incomparably better than those of the Canadian Pacific, and adjoined the Canadian Pacific tracks and yards. The Canadian Pacific Railway had a much better located passenger station. The officials themselves, in order to cut down expenditure during the war, met and agreed to combine the facilities. The arrangement was consummated before the public knew anything about it. The passenger facilities of the Canadian Pacific and the freight facilities of the Canadian National were to be used. It was a common sense arrangement, and has worked out well and to the satisfaction of the community, although the saving has perhaps not been as much as was hoped or anticipated. That is the sort of arrangement that should take place in a good many places in this country, with consequent elimination of duplicate services. All this question of amalgamation, or whatever you would call it, has receded into the background. No one hears anything more about it. Circumstances alter cases, and the question is not a live one to-day.
Coming back to the resolution, those of us who are not members of the standing committee on railways and shipping should have from the minister some definite information as to what really underlies this resolution. As I said this morning, a big railway system of necessity must have capital expenditures every year. It could not be otherwise. A portion of these capital expenditures is for refunding operations. These happen every year. But the membership of the house should be informed as to every aspect of the proposal underlying this resolution. And I am asking for information with respect to the refunding of equipment trust certificates.

I was not expressing myself very clearly if hon. members understood me to say that all this was justified only in connection with war purposes. If we want to cope with the present situation in regard to ordinary traffic, and also in regard to war traffic, we must have this equipment not only in Canada but in the United States. If the war had not occurred we would not require as much equipment, but these purchases are necessary partly for ordinary purposes and partly for war purposes.
My hon. friend mentioned the locomotives. We are providing for the transfer to Canada of twenty-five locomotives which are not entirely suitable to meet the necessities of the service on the lines in the United States but which will be quite sufficient to meet the necessities of the service in Canada. Therefore we are proposing to have twenty-five additiqnal locomotives built in the United States for service in that countiy. We propose to do this under an equipment trust by paying a certain amount of cash, as my hon. friend mentioned in his opening remarks this morning, and the balance in instalments. We are not building twenty-five locomotives in Canada. We could not, in war circumstances, readily build them here.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS

speechtext: Exactly. But I do not want to be taken too literally when I say this is required exclusively for war purposes. I may have gone a little too far in what I said previously in that regard, but the main expenditure is to cover the necessities of the war.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
My first observation is that I do not feel disposed to join in the mutual admiration society which occupied so much time, this morning. I hope the minister will understand that, and accept what I now say in the spirit in which it is offered.
For the last decade, ever since we first set up the committee on railways and shipping, time after time we have asked the management of the Canadian National Railways to set their accounts in the same order as obtains

C.N.R.-Guarantee oj Securities
in respect of class one railways in the United States. It has been suggested that they set up the depreciation necessary to take care of wear and tear, so that we might have at least some comparative statement when we were considering the statement presented by the management of the railways, and that which is placed before our committee.
At long last we have a recommendation in the report before us. The resolution states:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to authorize the Canadian National Railway Company to issue securities not exceeding $29,414,206 in principal amount to provide the moneys necessary to meet capital expenditures made or capital indebtedness incurred during the calendar year 1941.
When one considers the first sentence in the resolution he must remember that when the report of the committee on railways and shipping passes the house the auditors will have mandatory powers to set up a depreciation account, in accordance with the rules of the interstate commerce commission, which governs class one railways in the United States. The amount of depreciation mentioned at one point is $11,307,000. I am of the opinion it will be a good deal more than that. That will immediately find its way into the liquid position of the railways. As I gathered from the minister's remarks, it can be used for capital expenditures, and it is possible that it should be used in that way. Nevertheless, it must be earned, and if, as the minister intimated, it is not going to be invested, and will go into capital expenditures, then I have no complaint. But if it is set up on the balance sheet as being earned, and then invested, I say to the Canadian National Railways: "Do not come back to the house next year and ask us to discharge the entire deficit, a portion of which would be accumulated from the mandatory powers asked for by the auditors in setting up depreciation reserve."
Further on in the resolution we find these words: "To authorize the making of further temporary loans to the said company for interim deficits." If this depreciation practice is proceeded with during 1941 there should be no necessity of further temporary loans to the company to take care of interim deficits, or for loans to be reimbursed from the annual revenues; use the depreciation reserves. That is all I have in my mind with regard to that part of the resolution.
Let us consider the very necessary additions to rolling stock, a condition which has been brought about by the war. Page 6 of the annual report of the Canadian National Railways sets out w'hat is required to meet anticipated war requirements. Then it adds
that the following equipment was acquired: 5 mail express cars, 4 coaches, 25 baggage cars, 60 refrigerator cars, 150 ballast cars, 15 cabooses and 21 work units. Evidently that is just for the ordinary use of the system throughout Canada, and is not necessarily related to war requirements.
I have in mind a constructive suggestion, and I am wondering if the idea I shall place before the committee has been explored. It would seem that the increased service which the Canadian National Railways have had to give because of war requirements cannot be chargeable entirely to Canadian account. A good deal of the extra traffic which to-day is carried on the Canadian National Railways arises from United Kingdom purchases in the United States. Purchases made in the mid-western states pass through Chicago and then through Canada to seaboard, and are carried in equipment of the Canadian National Railways. When our railways are transporting United Kingdom purchases in the United States they collect their toll, and thereby their revenue position is improved. Have we explored the possibility of charging to the Hyde Park agreement or to the lease-lend bill the cost of the extra equipment required to perform that service for the United Kingdom? If they were so charged could we avoid the necessity of making these further purchases of equipment, or of having our friends in the United States lend such equipment to us?
I have in mind the fact that taken as a whole our equipment is in good condition. With the cessation of hostilities the extra business we are now enjoying will disappear, and we shall have on hand a tremendous amount of equipment. That will have to be paid for, and it is possible that at the close of hostilities we may not be in too good a position to make payment of our maturities.
May I make one or two observations respecting attempts made in this chamber to get some conception of what is involved in the publicly-owned railway, and what was in the minds of some of us respecting the railway itself. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) said he believed there were some who would still like to see this property revert to private ownership. When he made that statement someone in this corner interjected, "Where would they get the money to pay for it?" My opinion is that private funds are not available in sufficient quantities in any one repository, or in any group of privately-owned organizations, to purchase the Canadian National Railways.

But the cheers echoed right across this chamber, the "hear, hears" and the "yea, yeas". In those days the minister was not charged with the responsibility of the conduct of the Department of Transport, and at least he did not dissent. I cannot recall any dissenting speech on his part. However, I am not going to thresh old straw; I merely mention this to show that it is impossible to keep a problem of this kind out of politics. I use the word "politics" in the higher sense, if it is possible to use it in that way. When a minister makes a statement, whether in St. Henri or elsewhere, whether he is the head of the Department of Transport or of any other department, his voice is listened to across Canada as well as in the province of Quebec. Those who are charged with the management of the railways, from the personnel on the payroll up to the directors, do not need to throw up a straw in order to see which way the wind is blowing. They cut their coat according to their cloth, as we all know. It is just plain common sense; it is an attempt to follow out the ideas which emanate from this house and which are announced by those who occupy the treasury benches.
If that is so, and we will admit it, speaking on my own responsibility and not for the party with which I am associated or for any other group, I make this suggestion. The minister more or less sits in with the directors of the railroad. There is a number of groups in this house; why not appoint from time to time two members of this house to act as directors

of the Canadian National Railways for a dollar a year? Why not let them sit in with the directors and become acquainted with the railway problem? I hesitate to use the word "farce", but that is what it really is when we are asked in the short space of two or three weeks to try to analyse the statement and to know all about the Canadian National Railways.

speechtext: I referred to propaganda outside the 'house.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
I recall that the minister referred to propaganda outside the house. I submit that the foundation of the propaganda outside the house and the propaganda itself are two different things. Let me speak first of the foundation for the propaganda. In 1917 we had a number of disjointed railway lines spread across Canada and the people who depended upon those lines for their connection with other parts of Canada expected that they would continue to operate. Some lines served very remote parts of the country, and the people expected that the service would be maintained. There was a universal demand that these lines be placed under public ownership. That was the condition then. The condition now is that we have a rather good system. It is an expensive system, and portions of it are not economical, but in the main it is a good system. It is a good system because we have been extravagant during the last decade in the purchase of equipment. The rails upon which the heavy cars and engines operate have been renewed, and in the main the system is in first-class order, certainly as compared with its condition in 1917. With regard to to-day's expenditure I come to my next point. There is a marked difference between conditions then and conditions now. In 1918 the United States was in the war. When the war was on and after, the New York market was open for borrowings, and we did borrow millions; we got into the billion figure. We were able to get all the money we wanted-quick money with which to discharge our obligations at that time.
The position to-day has entirely changed. Due to the neutrality law of the United States, the Johnson act, our friends in the United States are unable to lend us money. It is true that they have gone a long way in
helping us with the lease-lend bill, and I hope the railway system will take advantage of anything they can obtain in the operation of that legislation. But that is not enough. We are still short of several hundred million United States dollars, and while the present acts are on the statute books at Washington, we have no place to go to get that money. So to-day, as I say, we are forced by sheer necessity to avoid all possible capital expenditures in the United States for railway supplies. Down in the maritimes, instead of doubletracking their road they are putting in safety equipment to the amount of a million and a half dollars, with the intention of assisting the movement of freight. The minister knows, I believe, the item I am referring to. Where is that equipment coming from? Rochester. How is it paid for? With United States dollars. There is a direct obligation upon the foreign exchange control board to provide a million and a half United States dollars. The degree of that necessity, in my opinion, should be measured against the necessity of providing United States dollars for war equipment, and the question should be given very serious consideration.
I turn to the next point, having reference to retirements of obligations which are coming due. As the statement is drawn this year, there is no analysis showing what part of this money has to be paid in Canadian dollars, or in sterling, or in United States dollars. For our convenience all these sums are shown in the same kind of currency. The minister should make a statement of exactly how many United States dollars we shall have to find this year, not only to meet the purchases which are being made, but to retire maturing obligations. As I have said on a previous occasion, every possible United States maturity should be renewed rather than paid off. I made a general criticism of the conduct of the treasury benches during the last three or four years, and part of that criticism is related to the Canadian National railway accounts. The first war cloud showed up some four years ago, or it may be more exactly dated about three years ago, when the Prime Minister made a statement to that effect, and the mistake which the treasury has made ever since that time was in not seeing to it that every dollar coming due in New York from then on, instead of being paid off, instead of our banks and insurance companies using the money we had in our tills to pay it off, and then tying up the cash by floating more Canadian bonds, should have been renewed. The net result of that mistaken policy is that to-day our till is bereft of liquid capital, and a great deal of that bereavement is chargeable to the fact, that,

C.N.R.-Guarantee of Securities
not only the railway maturities but all other maturities which have come due in New York during the last three or four years, were paid off Instead of being renewed. They were paid off because our banks and insurance companies were short of investments and thought they would like a few more Canadian bonds. And now, those obligations having been paid off, and having no chance of borrowing in the United States, we must endeavour at this late day to renew any obligations which are maturing in the future. There are very few such, but I emphasize that, no matter how few they are, they must be renewed in New York if at all possible.
To summarize the ideas I wish to leave with the minister: Conserve every possible United States dollar for the purchase of essential war equipment, even if you have to put a check-rein on the directors of the Canadian National Railways. Keep in mind the possibility of using the lease-lend bill operations for the carriage of United Kingdom purchases, whether it be the expense of carrying the material or the capital cost of the extra equipment necessary to carry it. Borrow as much equipment as you can in the United States and avoid the necessity of new purchases. And then-speaking personally for the moment-give consideration to placing on the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways two, or three, or if necessary even four, members of parliament so that they can take a special interest in the people's railway problem. After all it is the people's problem. Our directors, who are doing a good job for us, perhaps have not the same perspective as we have here, and they have no more responsibility than we have. In turn, we could interpret their ideas, perhaps, a little more ably and accurately to our fellow members of this house; the family might be a little happier, and they would not be coming here so anxiously to get their legislation passed and get away, if they have to sit morning, noon and night, to accomplish their object.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: May I ask the minister if anything in the resolution refers to the Hudson Bay railway?

speechtext: No.

speechtext:
I notice this sentence
in the resolution:
-to make provision for the purchase or refunding of capital obligations of the company or of any company comprised in the Canadian National Railways system. . . .
The Hudson Bay railway is operated by the Canadian National Railways, is it not?

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS

speechtext: There is an item in the estimates for the Hudson Bay railway.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
In the purchase of
equipment, rolling stock, and so on, does the railway buy the equipment outright? Does it rent a considerable amount of equipment, or does it buy it on time? Is it financed by one of the United States finance corporations, such as the American Guarantee company, the Chase National bank, or a similar institution? I have seen on certain of our engines a little plate stating that the engine is the property , of one of these organizations. It has always seemed to me that a government institution, at least, should not be buying on an instalment plan, with the interest and other charges which are involved in that form of buying. Is any of our equipment purchased in that manner? If so, why should we do that, when it is a government institution ; and, particularly at this time, why should we be paying dues to a United States corporation, in view of all the difficulties of exchange? If we are doing that, why not pay the balance owing and discharge ourselves of obligations which cause a good deal of concern at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: My understanding, Mr. Chairman, is that we only supply or vote the money to the Canadian National, and they themselves buy the equipment they require. I am informed that for a very long time there has been no issuance of money for the purchase of anything in the United States.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: I do not mean buying in the United States; but do we purchase any equipment through finance corporations of the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: No. The railways do that directly, and they own outright anything they buy.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
That is
hardly correct. Under Sir Henry Thornton the Philadelphia plan did operate, and it is still operative, although no new financing may have been done, in that way. This is a well

C.N.R.-Guarantee of Securities
understood plan much in favour with the railways, and it has its advantages in financing the purchase of railway equipment. All railways do it, and they know their business in respect to matters of the kind. I am not criticizing it. All I suggested was that we had not paid annual instalments out of operation but refunded these amounts, and they are allowed to go into the debt of the railway. They were in days gone by, at any rate, and they will be there long after the equipment is worn out. It is not good business.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: We are at present providing, out of the fund which will be accumulated this year, $9,000,000 for the retirement of equipment.

speechtext: For two years they have been doing it.
