maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: I do not think I can say very much in answer to the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris). He made certain representations that may be well worth considering, and I cannot go further than to say that I will make note of them. My hon. friend complains about the provision, in the bill which is to be introduced, for the temporary deficit in the operation of the railway. This is necessary because, as I am informed-I have a good deal to learn in these matters-in the first part of the year the Canadian National Railways cannot meet out of cash all expenditures, but by the end of the year they have sufficient revenue to cover advances made them by the government to meet a temporary deficit.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: They have a large working capital.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
No. That is the explanation given me. The hon. member for Danforth also referred to the fact that the central traffic control, which was proposed to be established in the maritime provinces, was United States equipment and had to be paid for with United States dollars. That is perfectly true, but we could not procure the equipment elsewhere. What is the position of the minister or even that of the directors? To whom can they go for proper information to guide them in their decisions? They have only one course to follow, and that is to give heed to the' representations made to them by the officers and the technical employees of the company. If they do not go to these informed persons, to whom can they go? It is all very well to say that our judgment in parliament may be as good as the judgment of a man working for the railways. On certain questions I entirely agree with that view. But when it comes to 14873-225
technical matters, to purely traffic questions, I must confess that I do not feel qualified to balance my judgment against the judgment of the technical officers of the railway. We must take someone's word if we are to have a proper administration of the railways.
My hon. friend also complained that the procedure in the railway and shipping committee was not very satisfactory, that we are looking into accounts after the expenditure is made. That is true, but I wonder how it can be avoided. Speaking almost entirely as a layman, I submit that the Canadian National is more closely watched in its expenditures than any privately-owned organization, because at a meeting of a great corporation-we all know what it is-the shareholders have not the same means or facilities for acquiring information, nor have they the requisite audacity to go through all the statements of expenditures and to crossexamine the officers of the concern, as members of parliament have an opportunity to do. It is true there have been delays, and we have always had some complaints in that respect. There may be room for improvement there. Taking the system as a whole, however, while it may not be perfect it is to a large extent quite efficient, and provides the proprietors, the Canadian people, with a greater amount of detailed information than the ordinary shareholder of any large private organization ever receives. There may yet be room for improvement. I am not disputing my hon. friend's suggestion.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Simply to preserve the sequence of the record, may I point out that this statement was issued at Montreal on March 19 and two months and one day thereafter, May 20, members of this house began to consider it. Why should there be a delay of from one to three months in every year?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
I am not objecting to my
hon. friend's observations, nor am I prepared to say that there is no foundation for some of his criticisms. I am speaking of the situation as a whole and I am trying to explain that with all the imperfections of our organization in connection with the Canadian National the people of Canada are more fortunate than the ordinary shareholders of any large private organization in the country.
The hon. member for Danforth said that we should renew the bond issues that we have in the United States instead of discharging them, because that will cost more. I understand that at present we are experiencing some difficulty in making new issues in the

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: I wish the minister would clarify some figures with regard to the Montreal terminal. I may tell him that in Toronto the building of the Montreal terminal at the present time is a cause of considerable grievance, so much so that I ask the minister to give me figures. When I was in Toronto during the Easter recess I found myself in the position of having to defend the Liberal government. Everyone said, what about the Montreal terminal? I should like the minister to give me a good brief in the matter. In particular the minister made the statement that it was a shame to have this tremendous uncompleted asset in Montreal in such a state that it could not be used unless a few more millions, I think $2,000,000 was mentioned, were spent upon it; if that were done, it could be made useful. I find, however, according to sessional paper 92D tabled on March 26 last, that the sum of $3,599,000 was spent on the Montreal terminal in 1940. We are appropriating $4,100,000 to be spent during the present year. On top of that the dominion government appropriated under the heading of unemployment relief a further $1,500,000 which was spent partly in 1939 and partly in 1940; I think it is all spent now. Altogether that makes the substantial sum of $9,200,000 to complete the Montreal terminal since the beginning of 1940-we leave aside the few months of 1939 following the declaration of war. If my figures are correct it is quite evident that this very large sum was spent to complete the terminal during the last two years, which sum might better, in the judgment of many of us, have been retained for war purposes and the completion of the terminal left until the war is over when we may need to find work for the returned men.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: When I said that $2,000,000 would complete the Montreal terminal I had in mind new expenditure, new disbursements.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
New
commitments?

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:

These amounts of $1,500,000 and $30,000 are in addition to the figures I have just given.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
I should like to say a word and make a suggestion to the minister. The improved earning power of the Canadian National Railways last year was not due to any normal growth of business, nor was it brought about by any improvement in the management of the railway. It was due to an abnormal condition brought about by our war effort. We have no reason to believe that this increased business will continue after the war is over; on the contrary we have every reason to believe that after the war railway business will return to its former level, conditions will be difficult and we shall be faced with hard times. My suggestion is that the minister and the government should give consideration now to the problem that will confront the Canadian National Railways when the war is over, and should make plans to meet it. The time this problem should be considered is now, when conditions are

C.N.R.-Guarantee of Securities
comparatively good. The government should not neglect the matter because it is not pressing at the moment.
I had the honour of being a member of the standing committee on railways and shipping. When the president of the Canadian National Railways was giving his evidence before the committee I asked him this question:
Are the directors looking ahead to the time when peace will come again, with a view to adopting methods or policies to improve the position of the railroad after the war?
In reply the president said:
I think the experience of the war in respect to the increase in traffic and the improved financial result clearly indicates that what is wrong is the lack of traffic, and I do not see what the directors can do about that after the war, as it will depend entirely upon the conditions that obtain at that time.
I then asked him:
In all probability after this war we will experience a depression and be up against hard times. Are you looking forward to improving that situation at all? Have you considered it?
His reply was:
My point is this: I do not see what can be done on the part of the directors or anyone else to anticipate that condition. We do not know what it will be, and if the circumstances are such that the traffic is greatly reduced I do not know how the directors or anybody else can produce the traffic.
To suggest that if we cannot get enough traffic we shall not be able to do anything, that we shall just have to go behind, as I understand we did go behind at the rate of about a million dollars a week, in my opinion is to adopt a defeatist attitude. I do not think the government want to adopt that attitude. This is a problem to which the minister and the government should give attention now instead of waiting until after the war, when it will certainly have to be faced.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: The leader of the opposition has objected to this bill because, as he says, it is likely to interfere with our war effort. I think that is a very reasonable stand to take.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: I did not object to the bill. I think the bill is inevitable, but I wanted certain information about it.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
He objected to the rebuilding of this station; I believe that was a reasonable stand to take, and I agree with it. The hon. leader also said that it would be a good thing to leave all these projects until after the war, when they could be used to absorb some of our unemployed. The hon. gentleman who just took his seat referred to the inevitable depression that will follow this war, but what guarantee have we that 14873-225 V
the next depression will be regarded at all differently from the previous one? Before the luncheon recess the minister said this station had not been built before the war because of the depression. And why was nothing done during the depression? There was only one reason. Here were hundreds of thousands of men willing and able to do the actual construction work; miners, steel workers and so on all down the list, were looking for work, but nothing was done. Why? There was only one answer: because there was no money. And there was no money because, as the Minister of Finance told us on Monday afternoon, neither the government nor this house has any control whatever over the financial policy of this government. That is the reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: I deny that I made that statement, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Well, the Bank of Canada controls the financial policy of this country, and certainly the Minister of Finance told us that neither his department nor this house had any control whatever over the financial policy of the Bank of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
I deny that I made that
statement. I said the government had no control over the internal operations of the Bank of Canada.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Well, if I did not say that I meant to do so. We were talking about the internal operations of the bank at that time. I find that this matter was discussed at great length in the banking and commerce committee of 1939, and at that time the phrase used was "day to day operations." I had no intention of announcing any change in the policy that was laid down at that time. The distinction between having something to say about monetary or financial policy, and the government controlling the day to day operations of the Bank of Canada, was made very clear in 1939. Just before six o'clock the other evening I was the object of some rapid questioning here, and it may be that I went further than I should have gone. I have not looked at Hansard to see what I said, but I want to say to the members of the Social Credit party right now that I do not want them to attach any significance to any statements I made at that time in so far as they were at variance with the clearly established rule and policy laid down in the banking and commerce committee in 1939.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
I am not blaming the minister, but I should like to quote his words.

C.N.R.-Guarantee of Securities

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: The hon. gentleman must accept the statement of the minister as to what he meant.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: I accept his statement as it appears in Hansard.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: The hon. gentleman cannot accept Hansard as against the statement of another hon. member of this house. When an hon. gentleman says that he made p, certain statement, and that what he said was so and so, any other hon. member must accept what he says.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: If the record is the other way I would raise a point of order at once.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Hansard is not the record of the house; and Hansard cannot prevail against the statement made by an hon member. Hansard is only for the convenience of the' public; it is not the official record of the house, and under the rules no one can challenge a statement made by an hon. member as to what he did or did not say.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Then this makes the case even worse, because if the government had control-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: Furthermore it is not permissible to quote anything said during a debate, other than the one now proceeding, which took place during the present session.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
I am not quoting from Hansard; and of course I must accept the minister's word. But having done that I say that if this government and this house had complete control of the financial policy of this country, that makes the case even worse. Not only did this policy of deflation prevent the construction of this station and hold up every other public work that should have been and could have been done when we had the men and the materials available; it also prevented us from rearming in order to meet the challenge that we must have known was coming. Let me quote from a letter written to the London Times by Admiral of the Fleet Lord Chatfield, with regard to the loss of the Hood:
The Hood was destroyed because she had to fight a ship twenty-two years more modern than herself. This was not the fault of British seamen. It was the direct responsibility of those who opposed rebuilding of the British battle fleet until 1937, two years before the second great war started.
It is fair to her gallant crew that this should be written.
The reason the navy was not rebuilt was the same reason the station was not rebuilt- because they had no money.
[Mr. Jaques.l
Let me quote the words of a Conservative member in the British House of .Commons uttered on April 9, 1941, during the course of the budget debate. Remember, this was a Conservative member-not a socialist or a social creditor. He said this:
There has been a lot of talk about the period after the war. Many think it premature to discuss what will happen after the war. I think it right to do so. We have the lessons of the last war before us. I well remember coming back from France in 1919. This country was richer and had a higher prestige than ever before in its history. We had the greatest navy, the greatest air force, and the finest army in the world. We had the land of England better cultivated than it had been for two generations. We had more skilled mechanics, more skilled shipbuilders, in the country with magnificent new factories and machinery. The whole world was clamouring for our goods, and primary producers throughout the world had good incomes because prices were satisfactory, and they could pay for our goods, and they were demanding our goods. Our position was of immense wealth, but financial theory said: "You are poor," and for 20 bitter heart-breaking years we laboured to make the actual facts fit financial theory. Prices of primary producers throughout the world were forced down by our financial policy of deflation, we ruined the farmers of the world and the farmers of our own country. We destroyed shipbuilding yards, pulled down factories, scrapped machinery, forced our skilled mechanics and artisans to migrate to America and the Dominions; we made the soil of England go out of cultivation and become more derelict than it had been for hundreds of years. And at the end of 20 such years of bitter and hard work, we had made the actual facts fit the financial theory, and we were poor indeed and unable to keep up adequate armaments, and our prestige sank almost as low as it had ever been.
May I again remind the committee that these words were uttered by a Conservative member of the British House of Commons. One might say that anyone speaking there is facing death at any moment. In fact it was shortly after those words were spoken that the House of Commons met with the same fate as the Hood-and for the same reason.
There is a confession. When I hear any hon. member either on this side of the house or on that side make a similar confession, I shall have some faith in what is intended for this country after the war is over-and not before.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
I was interested to hear the minister tell us in his usual impassioned way how fortunate we were as a Canadian people to be shareholders in the Canadian National Railways. I believe the records will prove that our fortune has been largely limited to the matter of paying annual deficits.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: It will be done in the usual manner.

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS

What will be the

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS

Not even within 2 per

maintopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
It seems too bad we
cannot have that information,' because the resolution provides for the guaranteeing of the interest and principal of securities. I had expected to hear someone ask why we had to go on the open market for this money- money which will be guaranteed by the federal government, and which would be an absolutely gilt-edged security. Why should we have to pay interest to outside concerns? I cannot understand it. Why not use our own Bank of Canada? The people of Canada are beginning to wonder why we should have to pay interest from our tax revenues on guaranteed funds, when we are borrowing money guaranteed by this government. There can be no reason. Why should there be rates of interest, and why should we not know what rates we are going to guarantee?

speechtext:
As a public ownership supporter I have been considerably interested in this resolution. During the last election, I believe both parties had a policy. This is one of the most important problems we have to consider, and it is unfortunate that more time is not given to its discussion in the house. We took three weeks on wheat. A select committee was appointed one day without notice being given on the order paper, and it has made two or three reports. Every Canadian is a shareholder in this road, and it is unfortunate that more attention is not given to this matter. Look at the interest that has been taken in public ownership and public utilities in Ontario. The financial statement issued there is just like a bank statement. This Canadian National railway system is made up of the old Intercolonial, the old Canadian Northern which should have been put into receivership, the old Transcontinental, the old Grand Trunk, and outside services in hotel and marine and other services and subsidies. It is a long Story.
Certain parts of the resolution do not conform to the policies which have been set out by two royal commissions. The first was the Drayton-Acworth, which sat in 1917, and the second was the Duff commission. One can learn little or nothing from the financial statement of this publicly-owned railway system. In my opinion the government made a great mistake in not having at the start moved t'he head office of this system to the city of Toronto. Ontario is a great public-ownership province, and the railway makes most of its money in that province.
I am a supporter of public ownership, but this is not real public ownership at all. It is the mistakes of private ownership from the start. The resolution shows that advances are to be made to subsidiaries which are operating at a deficit. It will be noticed that there is a difference in the way we finance the war and the way we finance these deficits, yet the war requires a much greater expenditure. In the case of the war, we are charging two-thirds to income and one-third to capital, reversing what was done in the last war; we are asking the people of the country to pay the greater part of this two-thirds by many new forms of taxation, although this generation suffer in flesh and blood as well. In this case many old debts are refunded from year to year, with a heavy interest burden. In my opinion there should be a different system of accounting and auditing and a different form of financial statement and set-up so that the workers and the business people of the country may understand the exact financial

set-up, and there may be a complete intelligent balance sheet easily understood by all.
So far as I can find out, since 1920 the deficits of the Canadian National Railways have taken $633,718,706 from the pockets of the Canadian taxpayers and no assets have been created. The Duff commission which was appointed in 1932 dealt with this matter of refunding and made a recommendation that in connection with the deficits of the system it was undesirable to issue securities guaranteed by the government, that the government should borrow the money and pay the deficits itself. I believe there has been some amendment to that. In my opinion the Bank of Canada should deal with this particular matter, be placed in charge of these securities, take care of deficits as a trustee, and consolidate these government and crown properties, and it should be consulted more regarding the financing of the whole proposition.
As regards the amounts the railways have made out of the war, it appears that $2,750,000 was earned by one railway and $2,500,000 by the other. The relief which would be obtained by the cessation of the annual deficits would aid in both peace and war to bring about prosperity; it would leave that much more money for the government to spend elsewhere, and reduce the annual tax rate. The fund now used to pay these losses would be available for other governmental purposes.
These deficits cannot be overcome by increased efficiency of operation. To my mind there is no evidence that, broadly speaking, this railway is not as efficiently managed as possible. There are some features which indicate extravagance and in respect of which no vision or foresight is shown, and the requirements by way of capital expenditure as set out in the resolution would be much less if such foresight had been shown. I have in mind the United States affiliations; I note how the luxurious cars in these trains compare with the cars in other trains within Canada, and especially those of the oldest rolling stock used in the transportation of troops.
I say, therefore, that the losses which are shown in the resolution will not be brought to an end by increased business. The railway is not progressive enough to recognize the inroads made by the motor bus as a factor in transportation. As a result, the railways have lost the cream of the business. Reduced mileage and cooperative effort between the two railway systems which will do away with unnecessary duplication of services constitute the only method of reducing the loss. There has been delay in acknowledging this fact,

C.N.R.-Guarantee of Securities
and a lack of courage in this particular matter. Compare the subject matter of this resolution with the way in which the railway problem is handled in the Union of South Africa, where new methods of operating and financing the railways, as to both capital and income, have been successfully tried also in the United States to some extent. In the great war that government took over the railways in the United States for the period of the war and consolidated services, and returned them afterwards to private operation, taking care of the deficits and charges in many ways as a war effort in part. In this country, however, little has been done under the statutes providing for coordination. Cooperation on a minor scale has not effected enough saving to meet the needs of the situation. The economies resulting from cooperation on a minor scale between the roads have had little effect in reducing the debt for either capital or maintenance. In nine months prior to July 1, the two railways cooperatively abandoned, were granted permission to abandon or were preparing to abandon 750 miles of lines estimated to bring about an annual saving of $647,040, but the total amount saved by the companies through piecemeal cooperation is only slightly under $2,000,000. In my opinion the amount asked under the resolution, $29,000,000, is too much, because only the surface of possible savings through coordination has been touched. Competitive lines are still being operated to take care of business which could be efficiently handled by one road.
Take the matter of the troop trains. I refer to the return I received to an order of the house, setting out the sums which I stated a few moments ago. I maintain that there has not been the coordination of services and cooperation there should be, and soldiers should be given better trains and services, and cut-rates much more than they are given.
The resolution makes reference to the refunding of capital obligations. Some of that debt is due to duplication of services in terminals and to equipment. In Vancouver one union station could easily take care of all business; yet two separate stations are being operated. The same is true of Winnipeg and more especially of the wastage on the Montreal terminal. In Toronto there are two or three stations. The one in North Toronto is practically closed and rented for the period of a year and one union station, while it effects many economies, is not what it should be. We all know the situation in the city of Montreal. The taxpayer has to pay for all this; he has had to hand over deficits averaging $45,000,000 or $50,000,000 a year for many years. I can
only say that so far as the revenues go, based on rates and returns per mile, per car mile, and all that sort of thing, the statement does not indicate very much relief for the taxpayer. I am sorry that we have not been given more information about the auxiliary services, namely, the hotels and the merchant marine. It would be a godsend if we had at this time, for use in the present war, all those fine merchant marine ships which were sold for a very small sum of money five years ago.
Three or four reports have been presented by the committee which considered this $29,000,000 issue of securities. The third report has not yet come before the house.
I hope that an opportunity will be given to deal with it, because in my opinion, if report No. 3 is a sample of the committee's work, they are not dealing with the facts of this situation from a commercial or business point of view, but are considering in their report solely the questions from the political aspect of carrying on and getting business for the branch lines and all the other projects which in their opinion have to be carried on.
We have had to suffer the consequences of the railway bungle almost since confederation. We have a railway mileage on two roads of
43,000	miles, equal to Germany, with a population of over sixty million, that of France, and that of England, whose population before the war was forty-six or forty-seven millions. I wish the national railroads every success. It is obvious that the taxpayer will again have to pay, and he should be given the facts. I believe the only proper statement I have ever seen was given -in 1937. The figures then stated may not be exactly applicable to the position to-day, because the deficits have been reduced. But a clear statement of the whole history of this road and all services was made by my former leader, Mr. Bennett, in the house in answer to three questions raised in 1937 by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Esling). It will take only a few moments to read those questions and answers, and I will therefore quote what appears in Hansard of January 29, 1937. The first question was:
1.	What is the total indebtedness of the Canadian National Railways to the public?
The answer was:
$1,184,612,248.59 at December 31, 1936.
The section question was:
2.	What is the total annual interest on this indebtedness?
The question referred to 1936. The amount has been reduced considerably since then, but the principal is the same. The answer is:
$49,184,622.87 in 1936.

I am in hopes that the government, instead of presenting all these 19-11 cumbersome statements, will be able to issue a clear budget such as is provided in Ontario in connection with public utilities developments, involving very large sums of money, of the hydro electric system. In the provincial and local hydro systems the method followed by the hydro board in making a report on the hydro municipal utilities gives a clear statement to the public. By means of page advertisements in the newspapers, the position of the Toronto transportation system and buses could be quite clearly presented.
As I have said, I wish the government every success in this operation. The time will come when some changes will have to be made. I am sorry to have detained the committee, and now, while I do not agree at all with his policies, I wish only to compliment the minister upon one thing; I am glad to see him this session with his health somewhat restored, and I know I am expressing the sentiments of every hon. member, because his health was said to be impaired

by overwork. I do not agree with all the minister has done, but I wish to pay him this tribute, and not only him, but I wish to pay tribute to the Speaker, the Clerk of the House, and the Chairman of Committees, the Deputy Speaker.
The Clerk of the House, by his vision, politeness, courtesy and efficiency has added greatly to the effectiveness of parliament, and I have found, over twenty years, the House of Commons to be a place of much kindness. I only hope the railway will consider these matters and that a better statement will be forthcoming. They are spending a great deal of money without any commensurate efficiency in some ways at times. I travel on the railway, and I can say that the service is not what it should be. The system is being starved, and no doubt for the money it costs it should be better. What is needed is a proper publicity department to put the facts before the people. There is, in connection with the railway, a publicity department which is costing the country a large sum of money, but the whole organization is not worth as much as it should be. All it does is to spend money on entertainment and on work that could very well be done without as an economy. The minister should consider closing the head offices in Montreal and moving them to Toronto. The Minister of Finance is sitting beside him, and I suggest that he should wield the big stick on the railway in this matter of expenditures, because there is too much expenditure and not enough efficiency to-day. An effort should be made to operate the system from the commercial aspect. The Minister of Finance should provide a part of the deficit from revenues without refunding a lot of money, which costs a great deal in interest rates. He should wake up the Canadian people to the fact that they are not getting the service to which they are entitled. There is duplication, waste and luxury in Canada's railway. I know that this exists in the other system, too, but the other system is a taxpayer while this is crown property. The people of Canada are the shareholders, and members of parliament, their representatives, should be able to go back to their constituencies and give a plain and intelligent statement of facts regarding the present financial condition of the road from the commercial aspect and every other phase of the railway.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Has the government succumbed to the importunities, or threats, or whatever you like to call them, of the premier of Ontario? I am prompted to ask that question because in this afternoon's Journal there is a statement that the government is introducing an amendment to the act which will cancel the recently imposed 15 per cent tax on interest from provincial bonds held by non-residents of Canada, and that the amendment will restore the tax to the former 5 per cent level. If that is true, it is a great victory for provincial rights.

speechtext: I have a statement to make in that regard. The hon. gentleman has not made it any easier for me to make that statement. I thought from his attitude the other night he was disposed to be helpful-

speechtext:
-but I do not think his statement was. I would ask the committee to follow the statement which I am about to make, because it is a matter of great importance.
Before proceeding with this section, I wish to make a statement with reference to the controversy which has arisen in connection with the application of the increased tax imposed on foreign holders of provincial bonds. On Tuesday last I placed on Hansard a copy of the telegram which was sent by the Prime Minister to the Premier of Ontario on May 30. As the committee will recall,
this telegram stated that we learned with keen regret of the attitude which Mr. Hepburn continued to take with regard to the increase in the tax on interest going to foreign holders of provincial bonds, and that as a result of the imposition of this increased tax the government of Ontario considered it necessary to reject the offer made by the dominion to the provinces in the budget of April 29.
The telegram went on to reiterate our conviction that the tax was fair and reasonable; that it represented only an increase in a tax that had been in effect since 1933 without protest from the province of Ontario; that it was low compared not only with taxes imposed on other income earned in Canada but also with similar taxes imposed on non-residents by the countries of which our foreign bondholders are citizens; that it constituted no threat to the credit of Ontario or of any other province; and that it was validly imposed and could be enforced. Nevertheless the telegram indicated that the government consider that it would be most unfortunate were there to be any serious controversy between the dominion and the largest and wealthiest province of Canada at a time when the major consideration of all Canadians should be the most effective and most united prosecution of the war.
What was viewed with particular regret was that under such conditions the government of Ontario should feel it necessary to make the increase in this tax on foreign bondholders its reason for refusing to accept the offer made to the provinces in the budget. Were the matter to be left in this position, it was pointed out that the citizens of Ontario would be prevented by prospective double taxation of their incomes from making as large subscriptions to the 1941 Victory loan as otherwise they would be able and willing to make. Since this government was anxious to remove any possible excuse for the continuance of such a situation, the telegram concluded by offering to restore to its previous level the tax on interest received from provincial bonds by foreign bondholders if the government of Ontario on its part would be prepared to give the dominion prompt assurance of its willingness to accept the offer which was made in the budget.
On Saturday last the press of Ontario carried a statement purporting to have been made by Mr. Hepburn to the effect that the dominion was tying up the offer made in the budget with the increase in this tax on non-residents, and that it had intended all along to use this increased tax as a device for securing the acceptance of the other offer. I think I made
Income War Tax Act

it clear beyond peradventure the other evening, that it was Mr. Hepburn who had tied the two things together and that we were only trying to remove what he himself said was his reason for his refusal to accept the offer I made in the budget.
While in the telegram of last Friday the Prime Minister had asked for prompt assurance with regard to Ontario's position, we have not as yet received any reply from the Premier of Ontario. We cannot very well delay any longer in proceeding with this bill. We do not propose to allow our motives to continue to be misrepresented or to allow the action of this government respecting one item of taxation to be cited as a reason for the non-acceptance by the government of Ontario of the offer we made in the budget. I wish, therefore, to advise the committee that after very careful consideration we have reached the conclusion that we should remove all possibility of doubt as to the respective positions of the two governments in this matter. Accordingly I propose to introduce an amendment to the bill as it stands, in the form of an additional section, the effect of which will be that in so far as this tax is concerned, absolutely no change will be made in the law as it stands now and as it has stood for the last eight years, in respect of the tax imposed on foreign bondholders as a result of the interest they receive from their holdings of provincial bonds.
This amendment will take the following form:
That the said bill be further amended by inserting after section 17 the following as section 17A:
17A. Notwithstanding anything contained in sections 16 and 17 of this act, section 9B of the Income War Tax Act shall, in the case of interest received from or credited by his majesty in right of any province, have effect as if the said sections 16 and 17 had not been enacted.
It will be noted that not only will the foreign holder of provincial bonds be left in exactly the same position as before, but also that there will be no change whatsoever in the rights and liabilities of his majesty in the right of any province. We believe, and we are advised1 by the Department of Justice, that by the law as it stands and has stood since 1933 the tax has been validly imposed on interest received by foreign holders of provincial bonds, but this has been challenged by the government of one province. It may be that in view of the proposed amendment the government of Ontario will not widi to create any difficulties in the collection of a tax to which they have not objected during the last eight years under peace-time conditions. If, however, they think the foreign bondholder should not only not share to

gome extent wit'h all Canadians the increased burden imposed upon Canada by the war, but should also be relieved from taxes which they have been paying in peace time, and if, therefore, they request us to test the legal position in the courts, we shall immediately submit a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada in order that the whole position may be clarified.
There will, I am sure, be some hon. members who will criticize the action which I am now proposing and will strongly contend that we should not make any change at all. On grounds of strict logic, on grounds of the fairness of this tax on the foreign bondholder, and on grounds of the country's financial needs, their position is one with which it is hard to disagree. On the other hand, we have had to weigh the larger issues involved. In the first place, it would be, I repeat, a great misfortune if in war time there should develop a serious controversy between the dominion and the largest and wealthiest province allegedly over the proposed increase in this tax by the dominion. The fundamental matter to-day is the united and effective prosecution of the war, and we should all be big enough to recognize that simple fact.
In the second place, the revenue which we would receive from the increase in this tax on foreign bondholders is a consideration of minor importance compared with the importance of the dominion not doing anything which could be cited by the government of Ontario as an excuse for its refusal to accept an offer which would save the people of Ontario from paying an extra $29,000,000 or thereabouts in taxes.
Finally, the question of taxation of this kind seems to be a highly technical matter, and it appears to be difficult to get to the people of Ontario an unprejudiced view of the relative merits and demerits of this tax proposal. It is extraordinary to me that this should be so, but when I read some of the statements which have been made about this tax increase I am forced to the conclusion that the position of the dominion government must be made so clear as to permit of no possibility of misunderstanding or misrepresentation.
It is for these reasons that I offer the amendment which I have read.
I wish also to offer an amendment to section 16:
That section 16 of the hill be amended by adding thereto subsection 2 reading as follows:
2. That subparagraph (ii) of paragraph (e) of subsection 2 of the said section 9B be amended by adding thereto the following:
"Provided that in the case of motion-picture films, one-third of such payments shall not be subject to the tax under this section."

Income War Tax Act
The gross tax on motion-picture film rentals was for several years 2 per cent. In 1939 it was raised to 5 per cent. By the increase under this budget that was multiplied by three, raising it to 15 per cent. I am convinced after exhaustive investigation, having spent a great deal of time on the matter, that 15 per cent is too high and that 10 per cent is high enough. Therefore I am moving that only two-thirds of such payments be subject to the 15 per cent tax.
It may be remembered that between 1936 and 1939 the ordinary rate was 5 per cent, and that that was subject to a deduction of 60 per cent. Therefore I am merely proposing that the 15 per cent be subject to a deduction of 33J per cent.
If the committee should ask me why I selected 10 per cent I could not answer; it is more or less arbitrary. But 15 per cent is a terrific weight when applied to the rentals of motion-picture films.

Under the Supreme Court Act no question can go to that court unless there are two. parties to the issue and a text to the reference. The reference in this case, if it goes to the supreme court under the Supreme Court Act will be the Attorney General of Ontario versus the Attorney General of Canada. I suggest that, since the same matters are involved, there should be a reference to the court not only of this particular question to which the minister refers if Ontario consents, but also on death duties and income taxes, about which there are grave doubts as to the powers of this parliament in view of the provisions of section 92 as to property and civil rights in the provinces and other sections. I suggest that these matters be included in the text of the reference as well; they are co-related, and also that the Minister of Justice, if there is a reference as a matter of law and public policy, should lay the text of it on the table of the house.

I wish to say a few
words regarding the announcement the Minister of Finance has just made. I appreciate the difficulty in which the minister finds himself; but on behalf of what I believe to be a very large number of people in this country I wish to register a most emphatic protest against the release of foreign bond holders from the taxation which was proposed. We are at war, and it seems to many people that the burden of the cost of the war must be spread over all who can share the burden; not only who live in Canada but who have an interest in Canada. That, I believe, is a fair view of the situation.
I was a spectator at the dominion-provincial conference. There I heard the minister make it very clear indeed, not as a threat-I think anyone who was there realized that no threat was made or intended-that because of the failure to straighten out certain constitutional matters in the discussion of the report and recommendations of the Rowell-Sirois inquiry, the necessities of war would compel the dominion to enter into fields then occupied by the various provinces. This naturfilly was one of the fields contemplated; and I am of opinion that in spite of the fact that the government has been obliged to take this step as a result of the attitude of the premier of the largest province of this dominion, we should not let this occasion pass without registering our protest against any provincial premier interfering with our vital efforts to raise the revenue that must be obtained for the conduct of this war. Those who are giving lip-service to the Dominion of Canada's war effort ought to be prepared to do more than that; and if there is one province that is in a position to assist the government in every way, it is Ontario.
I am not going to enter into a discussion of the attitude of the premier of Ontario; but I have felt, as many others have felt, that all too frequently Mr. Hepburn speaks and acts for certain interests outside the Dominion of Canada. In this instance I think, on the very face of it, that would appear to be the situation. I wish to make a most emphatic protest against the government taking this step. As I say, I know the necessity is great; I realize that we must get this tangle straightened out, but I believe I speak for a number of people in this country when I say that the primary place to get money for our war effort is from accumulations of wealth. I believe those who have accumulated wealth invested in the Dominion of Canada ought to be prepared at this time to share the burden with those who reside in this country.

I wish to register, just as emphatically as possible, an opinion directly opposed to that expressed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I do not think the
Minister of Finance should feel so very badly about giving way to the Premier of Ontario. I approach this problem from an entirely selfish point of view; that is, selfish from the point of view of the dominion or the province. These obligations which are expressed in terms of United States currency were created because we required the money to carry on our operations in Canada, or to carry on industrial development, or to construct public utilities such as the hydro electric and other similar enterprises. After the war is over, probably the time will come when we shall want to go back to the United States and borrow for development purposes, and in order to provide work for Canadian workmen. The question is not whether United States investors should bear their share of the burden of Canada's war effort. They bought these bonds on the understanding, perhaps implied on their part, that they would receive the full amount indicated on the coupons. Already these investors are faced with a discount, of 11 per cent by reason of the fact that our money is worth that much less than United States money; and if the 15 per cent provided in the original resolution had been added, it would have meant a discount of 26 per cent on the securities held in the United States. I do not mind this tax of even 15 per cent being applied to those who receive dividends on common stocks, the proceeds of which were invested in Canada, because they took their chance on the development of this country, and they expected to make a profit or receive an income higher than the bond return. Therefore they must in all equity bear their share of the expense of protecting that investment in this dominion.
The position of the bondholder is, however, somewhat different. Therefore, when we approach this problem from the selfish point of view of Canada, we must realize that we shall again require money from the United States for development, and there is no use in antagonizing the United States investor more than we need to. I believe, however, the publicity which has been given
to this 15 per cent tax has been out of all proportion to the feeling against it on the part of certain United States bondholders. It has become somewhat of a political tempest in a teacup.
I believe, however, the government of Canada may find it is doing a very good service to this country, and not merely obliging the premier of one of our provinces, in taking the attitude which has been indicated. There will come a day when we shall want capital. When the United States investor in our securities looks at the position in Canada he will not conclude that we have yet reached the limit of our own sacrifice, or that we have reached the point where we must place a tax on the United States investor. He will see that in our ordinary everyday life we do not seem to have had to sacrifice a great deal. It is true that there have been substantial financial sacrifices on the part of some, and others, of course, have enlisted in the armed services. I am speaking, however, of ordinary civilian life.
If the minister says that we do require money and that we must place a tax on the United States holder of our securities, then why not impose a 50 per cent tax? Possibly that could not be done in fairness, but the legal position would be much the same. Of course it is absurd.
I believe the policy which is now being adopted will redound to the material benefit of our country.

I do not wish to interrupt the discussion, but I should like to say a word about that portion of the amendment relating to films. I recall that in 1936 the then Minister of Finance, Mr. Dunning, reduced 'the remittance tax on films, particularly and specifically, from 5 per cent to 2 per cent. The plea at that time was that after the films were used throughout Canada they were useless, and that, therefore, the film agencies were losing large sums of money.
In what I am about to say I shall refer to the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce, a government publication in black and white. It goes on to show that the films which we see thrown upon the screens are not the actual films brought into Canada. They are only prints. The actual film is a negative, and it is sent to a processing plant in Montreal. I suppose that it enters Canada in bond, and for purposes of valuation it is valued at five cents a foot, the rate of tax being 32^ per cent.
The negative goes to the processing plant in Montreal, and from it as many prints as are required by the agency are made, the negative then being returned to the owners or producers in the United States. The business with the various theatres or film agencies which, in 1936, numbered sixty-three, is done as between those agencies and the processing plant. The agencies pay the processing plant. Taking for example a standard film of seven thousand feet, we find they pay a processing fee of three and a quarter cents a foot, plus sales tax. Therefore each print as shown upon the screens of the various theatres represents something like $246, and no more. One would think that that sum would be taken in during the first showing in a large city

Returning to the report of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, we find that the total revenue from rentals to theatres received by the various film agencies in 1938 amounted to something like $8,500,000. I believe that is the last year for which we have the figures. The amount may have been $8,000,000. The report goes on to show that they take from that about $1,060,000 for wages and about $2,500,000 for cost of distribution of films to theatres across Canada. It shows, too, that after all these deductions, the film agency had at least $5,000,000 to remit to the picture producers in the United States.
One can see at once, therefore, that inasmuch as these are only prints, there can certainly be very little loss. It is also difficult to understand why the remittance tax affecting the picture producers in the United States should be decreased while a small United States investor in a Canadian mining property pays the full remittance tax.
It was on those very representations, taken from the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce, that either last year or the year before the Minister of Finance put the film tax back to 5 per cent. I am wondering whether those who offered the suggestions have had an opportunity to go through the figures in the report I have mentioned.

May I point out to the Minister of Finance that I had no intention of implying that I was opposed to the imposition of a tax on bonds held by non-residents. I think the remark made by the leader of the opposition needs a little explaining. For the life of me I cannot see why the dominion should impose a tax upon provincial bonds, and not one upon dominion bonds, when both are held by non-residents. This will certainly affect the credit of the provinces. As the leader of the opposition says, it may be necessary for the dominion to go to foreign countries in order to get money, but I think we have a great deal more money here in Canada available through our Bank of Canada if necessary. If, however, it is necessary for the dominion to go to foreign countries for more money, it will be equally necessary for the provinces to do that. If the dominion has no money for its own needs, it certainly will not have any for provincial use.
One of the greatest dangers is the fact that if the dominion should take this action, should discriminate as between provincial bonds held by non-residents and dominion bonds held by non-residents, to tax the one and not the other, it will be forcing the provinces to come to the dominion for any money they need. Tn that way there will be a further centraliza-

tion of financial control, making the provinces that much more subservient to the dominion. That is not the right principle to follow. In fact, I cannot see why provincial bonds should not be a better security than dominion bonds. After all, if it is true-I use the word "if" advisedly-that the provinces have complete control of their natural resources, then I cannot see where the security for dominion bonds comes in. Of course, when it comes down to the fine point I doubt that the provinces have that control. When that is challenged, they generally find they do not have it. This is a question of foreign exchange, and I can think of several ways in which we can get more foreign exchange if we are really serious about the matter. Again I use a word advisedly. We could save United States dollars, or perhaps I should say Canadian dollars, by using Canadian coal. The saving in exchange would amount to about $15,000,000 a year.

speechtext: 27. Marketing service. Live stock and live stock products, $519,037.

Some months ago the
government put through an order in council detailing the manner in which farmers must dispose of their wool, and setting forth certain regulations governing those who purchase that wool. Upon whose advice were those regulations made? Was it upon the advice of the officers of the department, upon the advice of the wool dealers, or upon the advice of the mills?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The provision was brought in by
the department but only after full discussion with the different organizations concerned and with their consent.

From what I can gather, those who were concerned with this matter, and perhaps asked for their advice, were more particularly the wool dealers, the larger wool buyers or those who control the wool market of Canada. Certainly no regulation like this was ever passed after the farmers of the country had been taken into the confidence of the government and their advice sought. For years the farmers have been privileged to take their wool to the various small mills or to have the dealers call at their farms and purchase the wool there, and in most instances these farmers have received a pretty fair price. Under this regulation, however, the wool may be sold only to some one who is in a position to grade it. Wool must be graded and the various grades designated, a report being made out, and the farmer is paid according to the various grades he has supplied.
There are thousands of farmers who have always looked upon their wool as a ready cash sale. Farmers have come to our plant, but we are not buyers of wool to-day because we are not prepared to set up a grading station, and most of the small woollen mills in the country are in the same position. The result is that the farmer is almost forced to-day to send his wool to the cooperative wool growers of Toronto. The name in itself is misleading. It is simply a name; it is not what one would think it would be, with the name, Cooperative Wool Growers Association. People send their wool there and receive part payment for it, and they have to wait a long time before they get their final returns. It is not a cooperative concern, as suggested by the name, in the sense that the farmer eventually gets paid in proportion to the profit made by the company. It is a privately-owned company.
In my office on Saturday morning was a farmer who had 1,500 pounds of wool. He had always taken his wool to one of the small mills or one of the larger ones in our territory. The larger mills now say they will not buy it because they would have to set up a grading station. There must be some one to grade the wool and designate the various grades, setting a price, and in that whole territory where there are many mills none of the mills will handle wool. In the old days the farmer took the wool to the mill. The mills that were making blankets would not grade the wool because they would put it into their blankets as it was. The farmer to-day is practically forced to send his wool to the cooperative wool growers of Toronto, take part payment and then wait for months for his final settlement.

We are so regulating and regimenting the farmers that they cannot sell or do anything without filling out a lot of forms and complying with various conditions which are rather ridiculous, and many of these regulations are made by men who have approached certain sections of business in the country without having a practical knowledge of what should be done. This has worked a great hardship on the farmer who raises anywhere from fifty to 2,000 pounds of wool. There are farmers with thirteen, fifteen twenty, thirty or forty sheep, and every time we make regulations such as these we force the farmers into the hands of those people who have been making money by farming the farmers. The sooner we do away with many of these regulations, the better it will be for the farmers. This regulation was ill advised, and it is certainly working to the detriment of those men who have a few sheep on their farms.

Mr: QUELCH: Will the minister define and explain the respective provincial and federal fields in the grading of poultry and eggs? I ask this question because, while the grain rates to the consumer may be quite satisfactory, so far as the producer is concerned I am confident that they are not. I have heard a great deal of criticism, from many prominent poultrymen, of the method of grading eggs at country points. I have carried out some experiments to see whether that criticism was justified, especially in the rush season at the height of production. We have graded and candled a number of cases of eggs, put the culls in another case and shipped them all, and there was practically no difference in the returns on those cases, which convinced me that, in the rush season at any rate, returns are based upon average instead of upon individual shipments. Can the minister give us any information on that point?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The grading of eggs is carried on under exactly the same conditions as the grading of butter or any other farm products. If the product is produced in the province where it is finally disposed of, it is the responsibilitv of the provincial government. They can, u they desire, handle that product, and the federal government would have nothing to do with it. If, however, the product enters into interprovincial trade, then it becomes the responsibility of the federal government, and likewise if it enters into international trade.
In actual practice, in order to overcome the difficulties inherent in the federal system the provinces have been following the practice of appointing the federal inspectors as their inspectors, and it is the federal inspectors and graders who do the actual inspection and grading of the different farm products, including eggs, butter, wool and so forth.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The situation is that last fall, as hon. members know, we undertook to deliver to the British government 425,000,000 pounds of Wiltshire sides. During the preceding year we had delivered about
330.000.	000 pounds. We estimated that this year we would be able to deliver the
425.000.	000 pounds, and therefore undertook to do so. Weekly deliveries during the winter months, beginning last October, ran very much higher than a year ago, and were even beyond the amount which it was estimated would be required to fill the new contract. It will be recalled that I announced in this house more than six weeks ago that this spring the British government asked us to complete our deliveries by an earlier date,

which meant that we were required to deliver within the year about 28,000,000 pounds more than we had contracted to deliver.
Last year the United States price for live hogs averaged three cents below the Canadian price. There was a gradual advance in the United States price during the winter, and about the time we were asked to increase our deliveries, prices in the United States reached just about the Canadian level and hogs began to move into the United States at various points, particularly further west. The price in Alberta, for example, is lower than in other parts of Canada, because the freight rate increases as one goes further west, but the price on the United States side of the line, in Portland, Seattle and other places, is sometimes even higher than the Chicago price. As a result, it is only natural that hogs should go into the United States at those points, and also over the mountains to Vancouver. There is also a tendency for hogs to move to the United States from as far east as Winnipeg at a much earlier date than would be the case in the eastern part of this country.
It was very important that we should deliver the full quota to Great Britain this year, not only because they need it so much but because we wish to establish ourselves as people who deliver what we contract to deliver. During the period we were negotiating with Britain, which negotiations brought about the higher price put into effect a short time ago of 85 shillings per 112 pounds as against the 80 shillings we were receiving previously, it became necessary to take some action in this regard. We can only estimate the number of hogs that will continue to come on to the Canadian market during the year, and in order to make absolutely certain that we would be able to deliver the full quota that we had undertaken to deliver this year, it was decided by the bacon board to say to the people of Canada and to the packing houses, "We think we in Canada should be satisfied for the time being with the same amount of pork products that we consumed last year," and I might add that last year we consumed more pork products than in any previous year in our history. Therefore the level which has been set for this year for the consumption of pork products is equal to the highest level we have reached in our history. For the time being, then, we are saying to those who deliver pork products to the trade, "We want you to deliver only the amount you delivered in the corresponding week one year ago."
On that basis the amount of pork being consumed in Canada to-day is reduced, to a

certain extent, below what it might have been if that regulation had not been imposed; and we are quite satisfied that under conditions as they now exist we shall be able to get along on that basis. But after the British price had been increased, the United States price continued to rise, and accordingly we added another 75 cents per hundred pounds of Wiltshire sides in Canada so that the price has been increased not only by the British government but also by the Canadian government. We are not certain how long we shall require to continue this regulation with regard to consumption in Canada, but it has been continued up to the present time.
That does not answer the question I asked, which was whether the government were taking any steps to see that the consumers are protected while the amount of pork available is restricted.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Of course, when you start to restrict the consumer you reach a point where you also restrict the producer with regard to the price he receives. After all, what the farmer gets out of the hogs he sells in Canada is the British price for the products sold in Britain plus the price received from the consumer in Canada, and those two prices are averaged in the proportion that these pork products are consumed in these two markets. About 64 per cent of our hogs are consumed in Britain and about 36 per cent in Canada; or, roughly speaking, about one-third in Canada and two-thirds in Britain. Therefore, if you increased the price of one-third of the hogs by three cents, and spread that increase over all the hogs consumed, it would mean an increase of one cent in the general price. I am not at all certain that we want anyone to step in and begin to control prices on our local markets too soon, at least in the interests of the producers of the hogs. Probably the Canadian people will accept the position, as I think it was accepted last night with regard to eggs, that we in Canada should be prepared to pay at least as much for the Canadian farm products we consume in Canada as the British are paying for them, and that in some instances we should be prepared to pay even more. Consequently I hope no one will start too soon to control prices of pork products or other commodities.

The point is that the price the British are paying has risen by approximately SI per hundred; the price being paid by the consumer in Canada has risen three to five cents a pound, yet the price the farmer receives has not gone up $1 per hundred.

It has nothing to do with price except that we have not suggested to them that they should pay more for the eggs than they are paying in some other places from which they get eggs. Rehabilitation Act. He might tell the committee the programme for the coming season. I went to the auditor general's report in order to obtain a few details with regard to the operations of the last year, but I am sure the minister would not care to have me read all the comments in the report in connection with the work that has been done. I must leave it there because I do not want to take up the time of the committee. I will say, however, that a great deal could be said by way of criticism.
Yesterday the minister had a bill passed through the house in short order, and at his suggestion there was no particular discussion on it, because he said we might ask questions with respect to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act when we came to the item for that act. We refrained from discussion yesterday. The act gives the minister considerable power to undertake small projects up to $5,000, and I should like him to give an outline of what it is proposed to carry out this year and what he proposes to undertake under t'he act passed yesterday.
May I refer to another matter. Will he make a statement with regard to community pastures. I have a clipping from the Leader-Post in which it is said that there was to be a conference of community pasture managers. In the auditor general's report the statement is made that there are thirty or forty managers of community pastures, and there are only fifty-four community pastures in the west. That is out of proportion to the number of managers that could do the work. As the minister said on a previous item, the reason for a reduction of $75,000 this year was the war. We might take that to heart with regard to this work. We have a war on our hands, and it should be the minister's endeavour to curtail in every possible way expenditures on this work. It has been going on for the last six years, and I notice in the auditor general's report that there are thirty-one employees in the work drawing over $2,400 or more each, some as high as $4,000, one or two in the neighbourhood of $6,000, and their expense accounts run from $200 to $1,500 and, ini one instance, to nearly $2,000. That is one thing I should like to impress upon the minister; we have a war on, and while this work may be essential in some respects, I think he could curtail to a great extent and save, I would suggest, maybe half a million or a million dollars this year on this work without doing any injustice to those interested or to the west generally. Would the minister give us a statement with respect to what projects he proposes to undertake during the coming season?

The salaries range

As a matter of fact, when we set up the pastures there was a regulation to the effect that only a certain number of farmers would be allowed in, until there was enough live stock to take up two-thirds of the capacity of the pasture; then, before more cattle, horses or other live stock could be added to that number, the committee had to agree to the increase, and also had to agree on how the distribution of that increase should be made. The next item is the purchase of land, land sales and records, $75,000. That is a decrease from the previous year, when the figure was $110,000. Then we supplied bulls to these pastures, in the same way that we supplied them to clubs under other policies, and the amount allotted for this item is $15,000. Reestablishment of farmers amounts to $50,000. There is no provision for federal

relief this year, nor was there any provision last year. Previously we had to pay some relief in connection with persons whom we were moving out of sub-marginal areas into other districts.
Then seed purchase and preparation, cultivation and harvesting operations on lands being irrigated by large projects, amounts to $100,000. That is, when these irrigation
projects are started we have followed the practice of operating some of these lands during the first year and seeding them down to alfalfa, so that, this land could be used by farmers as pasture land as soon as they took over the property. We have also seeded grain crops on some of the land, harvested them and, in some instances sold the grain. These lands are always sold to farmers on the basis of $10 an acre, under agreements which really never come to a final conclusion. In other words, the government always owns the land; the last payment is never made, and consequently the government is always in a position to prevent persons from getting control of all the lands and giving them a speculative value. Then there is grass seeding of community pastures; $20,000 in the Swift Current experimental farm district; $20,000 in the Scott district; $10,000 in the Indian Head district and $1,000 in the Brandon district, making a total of $51,000.
