This act applies particularly to the district from which I come. The Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act was instituted primarily for the purpose of assisting the people in the dried-out sections of western Canada. After four or five dry years, many people throughout the country, including many members of this house, said, "Well, that part of the country never should have been farmed; the people never should have been settled there at all, because it is not fit for farming." Even in that district we had people saying, "Probably the government made a mistake in asking us to come into this country and farm." Speaking in this house towards the end of the session of 1933-34, when the Conservative government was in power, I mentioned this situation and advised the government to make a thorough survey of that section of the country in order once and for all to settle the question of whether or not that area was fit for farming. If it was found to be unfit for farming, I suggested that they should move the people out of that district to some other part of the west. On the other hand, I said, that if that area was suitable for farming, then the government should go there and show the people how they should farm it.
I was, and still am, one of those who believe that that area should be farmed, that it was a good farming country. It is bound to have dry years; it has had them in the past and will have them again, but I was in that district for twenty years and had better crops there than I had in other parts of the west. It is true that for the last ten years we have had crop failures there, and we shall probably have them again, but I advised the former government that if this area was found suitable for farming, they should save every bit of water so that not a drop from that dried-out area would flow into Hudson bay or the gulf of Mexico. I said that we should keep all the water there, in order that we might have crops, because there is nothing wrong with that part of the country except lack of water. I said that we should dig dams and build reservoirs; that we should put in dug-outs and commence irrigation. Then I said that we should prevent soil drifting by strip-farming; that we should conserve the snow, and gather it together. We should plant trees so that the snow may drift round them. We should put fibre back into the soil by having our people sow grass in different sections.
The result of this was that in the next year, 1935, Mr. Bennett put into effect the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. He procured a site for a dam at Valmarie, and one at Eastend, and began operations there. Operations under the act have been continued ever since. It has been a great work and has done a great deal of good. We have learned many things, and particularly with regard to water. I claim that the great thing in connection with the holding of water is, in fact, the small thing. That is to say, the small dam, the little dug-out on the individual farm does more good than anything else. Anyone who has lived on a farm and who has hauled water four or five miles to water his stock knows what a great benefit it is to have water right at hand. These little dams and dug-outs give the farmer that water. They also enable him to irrigate a small piece of land, even if it is only a quarter of an acre, so that he may have a garden and grow a few vegetables. That does more good than anything else- more good, even, than the big dams.
We know that we have big irrigation schemes, but my opinion is that they are good only for purposes of show-window display. They show the farmer what can be done by irrigation. But if western Canada is going to depend upon irrigation, then the future of western Canada will not be very bright. That is all I have to say about the matter. All that the big dams and big irrigation schemes do is to show the farmer what can be done by irrigation. It shows them how to. go to work in the making of small dams and small irrigation projects on individual farms. Those small dams are good things; they are the things which are of great benefit to the farmer. I heard someone say in the house the other night that the building of community dams, and that sort of thing, had developed into a racket. So far as my district is concerned, it was not a racket. I do not know whether I have an honest electorate or an intelligent electorate, but I know that we had no racket in this connection; nor have we had any of the bigger community affairs.
We have no big irrigation schemes. My district is in the very centre of the dried-out area, and yet we have not had those big schemes. We have no big dams. We have small irrigation schemes put in by the individual farmers. We have many small dams and dug-outs, but they have all been constructed by the farmers themselves. They are not drag-line propositions at all. None of them had cats and tumble-bugs to pull stuff out of the bottom of the dug-out. This was all done by the farmer with horses.

I should like to see more of these small systems. Then, practically all the better farmers in the district are doing strip-farming. Fifty per cent of our land, is under cultivation and is sown to seed, and 50 per cent of it is summer-fallowed.
The hon. member will not be in on the bonus this year.

No. I might say that most of our farmers are sowing their grain, much the same as they did in other years. They are not reducing their acreage. They believe it is better to have wheat stored on their farms than to have nothing growing. They would rather have three or four thousand bushels in their granaries, in case we have another dry year.
Next we come to the matter of tree planting. All hon. members will realize that tree planting is of great importance. We have many men in western Canada who are familiar with the subject. I still believe, however, that a great mistake has been made in connection with the planting of trees on the bald prairies from which I come. In the first place, the wrong kind of trees have been planted, and, in the second place, they have been planted in the wrong places. When a farmer in western Canada builds his house he builds it on the highest part of his farm, but that is the very worst place to plant trees. Invariably, however, the farmer plants the trees round his house, so that they may serve as a wind-break. He should, in my opinion, plant his trees in the lowest spot on his farm. He should plant them down in a draw, so that the trees could catch and hold the snow, and thereby develop a place where he could have a garden. The farmer, however, plants his trees on the top of a hill, where it is more difficult to catch the snow because of the action of the wind. The snow is blown away and does very little good and, in that position, the trees can do very little to hold the snow. They are only something to look at.
I say, too, that the kind of tree which has been planted is wrong. Invariably the farmers plant trees which grow quickly, and they have shown a preference for Manitoba maples and poplars. Those trees grow their roots close to the top of the ground, they do not develop a tap root. The result is that in the event of an early spring, and a spell of fine weather, the snow melts; the trees-possibly because of tree instinct

imagine that the summer has come, and the sap goes up into the branches. Then, during the night cold weather may come back; the thermometer may drop, and the tree is frozen, splits and dies.
Not only that, but trees of that kind take moisture from the top soil, and in dry years

many of them die. I have seen dozens and dozens of beautiful hedges die out in dry weather on account of lack of moisture. If we would plant trees with tap roots, roots that go down straight into the ground, we would find that they would not be so quickly affected by the fine weather. The few warm days would not get down to the depth reached by the tap root. The result is that the sap would not come up until later; the tree would not be frozen and would not split. If we planted trees like the caragana, we would have much better results, because we know how well it grows, and the manner in which it develops its tap root. The same applies to the elm. It grows well in my section of the country. We need trees with tap roots which would go down into the ground, and live there even in dry weather, when trees living nearer the surface would be dried up and would die.
Then we have the other proposition, namely, the planting of grass, with the object of putting fibre back into the soil, and thereby preventing soil drift. Added to all that, we have had the project for the development of pastures. That is a good work. It has taken out of cultivation land which should never have been cultivated, and put it back into pasture. I commend the government for the work it is doing along these lines, although it requires some supervision. I hope to see the work continued, despite the fact that we are in the midst of a war. This is a development which is helping the farmer, and which has brought about a great change in the country. I hope it will be continued.

The hon. member who just resumed his seat has expressed my sentiments, although I would not agree with him in all he has said respecting irrigation. Possibly he has not had enough experience in that regard to appreciate its value. May I express my warmest approval of the minister's ideals in connection with rehabilitation work. So far as I have seen, I believe that his work has been well done, and that it will stand for generations after we are gone. Certainly it will greatly benefit western Canada.
Like the hon. member for Willow Bunch, I have great faith in the west, but it must be borne in mind that much of that land is in what is known as the Palliser triangle and probably should never have been settled. But now that it is settled, I do not believe in quitting. I believe that if we go forward with faith and put forward the amount of effort we need to put forth, we can make of that area one grand asset to the Dominion of Canada. The amount of money which is being voted here is not enough. I should have

been glad to see the minister bring down an appropriation of $4,000,000, and I would gladly have supported such a vote.
May I go on to urge that the minister continue to develop the larger areas of irrigation too? The dug-outs are suitable for certain areas. Indeed, I believe that each of the other activities in which the department is engaging and spending money are all good for the areas where they are. But there are some areas where it is not difficult to put a quantity of water out on land, which is fertile, and with a climate that is excellent, to develop a region where fine homes can be built which will be a joy and satisfaction to the minister and those associated with him as long as they live to see that good thing.
I wish once more to express my entire approval of the minister's plans and of the way he has worked them out, and to urge him not to be influenced by those who are talking too much economy. After all, let us remember that this war is perhaps only in its beginning. If so, we are going to need all the production that Canada can muster, perhaps long before this war is over. If it so be that we shall be blessed with an early termination of the war, we shall have these projects there; they will be good, and we shall manage somehow to raise the money to do the other things that are necessary.

I should like to
bring to the attention of the minister the condition of Long lake within my constituency. It is not for the reason that it is so situated that I bring it to his attention. It is one of the largest lakes in southern Saskatchewan and it is of importance to the people of the province as a whole. It has located on its shores several fine summer resorts. Its fishing industry is of considerable importance. It is a reservoir of many hundreds of square miles. It has been receding over a period of years, and in the last year or so, in an alarming degree. This is one place where expenditures could well be made in order to ensure that that lake shall not dry out and that moisture shall be conserved. I would ask the minister to let the committee know just what is being done in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Long lake is situated, as many members of the committee know, almost directly north of the city of Regina, perhaps thirty miles north, and there are on that lake a number of summer resorts as the hon. member for Lake Centre has indicated. The lake is about seventy miles long and varies in width. It is one of the largest storage basins in the settled section of Saskatchewan and has been under consideration in this
house on quite a number of occasions. Many years ago it was used for navigation. A boat ran the seventy miles north, carrying passengers and freight up and down the lake. At that time there was a dam built on the Qu'Appelle river just to the south and east of the lake. That dam was constructed in such a manner as to catch the water when it came down in the spring of the year and force it into Long lake. Then, during the summer months, for a considerable part of the time the water was allowed to run out of the lake again and down through the valley. The government of Canada has had one or two lawsuits as a result of having changed the course of the water and raised the water levels-

May I ask if the
Qu'Appelle river had a branch flowing into Long lake?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Yes; the natural flow of water did take that course. It ran into the lake in the early part of the season, and, as well, water was fed into the lake from all round. When the water reaches a certain level it starts to run out again down the Qu'Appelle. But the dam which was put in made that operation more effective than it was before. The dam has raised the water approximately six feet above the original level through forcing the water in.
There was a lawsuit many years ago by reason of the flooding of lands at the end of the lake for the purpose of making it possible to run the boat to which I referred, and the government as a result of the lawsuit had to pay $50,000. Later on, there was another lawsuit because the people below were not able to get water on to their hay lands at the proper time of the year. The water came down in June and, instead of helping to produce hay, helped to produce foxtail. The operation of the dam was accordingly changed to let the water come down in greater volume in the spring of the year, and ever since that change in the operation of the dam, the level of the lake has gradually been going down. During the drought years it has gone down to six feet below the level of the stream itself from the Qu'Appelle river into the lake, from which the water comes in, part of the time. An effort is being made so to operate the dam as to raise the level to some extent, but I am afraid that as a result of our experience, the effort may not be successful until we have years of greater precipitation than we have had in the last three or four or even ten years, during which period there has been a receding of these waters. Nevertheless the water has been running into that lake.
Supply-Agriculture

There have been some other things done on the river which affected the amount of water which comes in at least in the early part of the year, after these works were constructed. A dam was put across the Qu'Appelle river up where Moose Jaw creek enters the Qu'Appelle, directly north of the city of Moose Jaw. The water from Moose Jaw creek, if I understand the location of the dam, remains in that lake. That is what is known as Buffalo lake, and the drainage from the west that comes down the Qu'Appelle and down from the north from all the streams in that area also runs into that lake. Up to the present time this year there has not been the volume of water come down from Buffalo lake which came down before, and probably that has had some effect on the amount of water which has gone into Long lake this spring.
My view is that the amount of water which passes Buffalo lake this year and perhaps for some succeeding years will not affect greatly the level of Long lake. But we shall have to have a few years experience to learn to what extent that is true. It is not impossible to let the amount of water come down which would have naturally come down, and to let it come down over a longer period of time, because the dam 'Can be so operated at the end of Buffalo lake as to make it possible for that water to come down the Qu'Appelle and be run into Long lake through the operation of the dam at Craven.
That is the position at the moment. The committee which has been appointed by the summer resorts on the lake has been working on the problem, and I am to meet 'them when I go west after the session, discuss the matter further, and decide on any works that may be necessary to control the water in the interests of all the people living in that area.

Will the minister outline
briefly his programme with regard to the building of small dams? I understand that the department has a number of old applications before it to be dealt with. Is it the intention to accept new applications, and what will be the price paid? The minister will appreciate the fact that under the new agricultural policy there will be a swing back to the raising of stock. A great deal of new land will be used for pasture, land which to-day has no access to water, and it will be necessary that provision be made for the construction of dugouts on this new pasture land.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
In so far as the dug-outs for which there has been application in the past are concerned, our present intention is to make a survey of those which

have been actually passed and arrangements for the digging of which have been made, and to have those passed first; and if they take up the amount of money which is available, that will be all that will be proceeded with this year. I am, however, under the impression that a considerable amount of the appropriation will be left after we have dealt with these, and then we shall take the applications in the order that they come in from that time on, in order to have dug-outs constructed on the different farms. I may say that it is the intention, unless we are otherwise advised or convinced by the advisory committee, to insist upon getting back to the method which was outlined by the hon. member for Wood Mountain, and which he says has been followed largely in his constituency, namely, of having these dug-outs constructed as far as possible by the farmers themselves.

Is it possible to obtain the services of the inspectors or engineers to advise as to the construction of these dug-outs in the event of its not being possible to get financial help in the digging of them? Can a farmer get this expert advice and go ahead with the work even though he is not paid for it?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Yes. When farmers
make application for engineering advice with regard to the building of dams or the construction of dug-outs on their land, we give that engineering advice free. We prefer, of course, that the farmer should do the work without assistance from the government. In most instances-I would say in 90 per cent- the farmer, because others are getting assistance, insists on having it too, and assistance for construction to the extent of four and a half cents a yard on the moving of earth is given in those instances.

I should like to ask the minister a question about another phase of prairie farm rehabilitation work. I refer to the soil surveys. I believe that that work should be continued and extended into the northern area of Saskatchewan, and, perhaps, some re-surveys should be made. Probably one of the most valuable services which has been done to western Canada is the soil survey. Had we had information available earlier as to types and locations of various soils, we might have avoided many of the errors which were made in settlement in past days.
I mentioned this evening Doctor William Allen, who together with Doctor Hope made an economic survey of parts of Saskatchewan. I believe that an attempt is now being made

Supply-Agriculture
to relate the surveys of these gentlemen to the soil surveys which were largely supervised by Doctor Mitchell. I am wondering to what extent the work is proceeding and to what degree the officials who are undertaking this work in the capacity of soil scientists are within the department. Are they yet temporary employees, or are they now a part of the civil service? I believe they are doing a very valuable work not only for our province but for the entire west. I should like to see the soil survey made a definite branch of the service and every encouragement given to continue and extend these surveys. I have in mind at the moment the possibility that after the war other people will desire to go on the land. We have not, so far as we know, a great deal of good land now available for settlement; but we have a great deal of land, and if it were classified, and analyses made so that we would know for what it is best suited, we might be able to find homes for people who might not be able to find them for themselves.
One of the finest services performed for the province of Saskatchewan and for western Canada, has been done under the supervision of Doctor Mitchell, of the university of Saskatchewan. I should like the minister to say a word about this matter, if he would.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Soil survey work has been going on in western Canada, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar knows, for quite a number of years. It has been a cooperative effort as between the federal government and the provincial governments. Mr. Wyatt in Alberta and Mr. Ellis in Manitoba have charge of the work there, operating through the universities. In Saskatchewan the system has been worked on a rather different basis from that in the other two provinces. After the last war we had a considerable amount of money derived from overages from wheat. The overage fund was turned over to the three provinces. Saskatchewan set aside from its share of the fund about a quarter of a million dollars, and ever since 1926 they have been using the interest derived from that fund for soil survey work. All the province has been covered by that survey, and, in addition, there has been a survey of precipitation over the whole province. A map has been made covering the soil survey; a new map is in process of being made in which the moisture condition as related to the soil condition is mapped as well, and one can get a very full knowledge of the condition of any area by examining that map.
As a result of these surveys, there has been set up in the various provinces systems under which an attempt has beei made to get 14873-227
people off sub-marginal lands. In Alberta they have their special areas. They have been working at this scheme since 1922, and probably more people have been moved off sub-marginal lands in Alberta than in the other two provinces.
Since this particular plan has been put into effect, and since we have adopted the practice of setting up pastures on sub-marginal lands, we have taken approximately a million acres of land out of cultivation or out of the control of individual farmers and put it into these community pastures. By this means, about a million acres have been taken out of possible cultivation for the growing of grain. The position in relation to that is that we are spending about $68,000 out of this vote on that soil survey work. The provinces are going on with the work which they have been doing, as well. The universities are associated with us in this activity, and we are hopeful that within a comparatively short period we shall have a complete knowledge of the soil condition of all the settled portions of the three provinces.

Before this item carries, may I observe that the discussion has been almost entirely from the point of view of western Canada. Those of us from the east have great sympathy for the west. We in Nova Scotia have special reasons to feel sympathetic because so many of our people went out west and helped to build up that section of the country. But we in the east, too, have farm problems, and to us it is staggering what sums of government money have gone into the west for the benefit of agriculture, in comparison with what has been expended in the east.
At the head of the bay of Fundy we have a problem as great or greater than any now facing the west, with regard to water control. Ours, however, is the problem of too much water, rather than that of conserving it. The figures I have secured indicate that under this heading of farm rehabilitation, there has been expended up to the end of the fiscal year, 1940, $9,794,597. There was appropriated for the fiscal year 1940-11, $2,500,000; I am not sure whether the minister made a statement as to what amount was actually expended.
This vote is for a further expenditure of $2,500,000. This programme provides for 31,089 smaller water-control projects, a few of which have not yet been undertaken, and, in addition, sixty-three large projects. There are extensive irrigation undertakings; there are community pastures, grass seeding, soil survey, pasture survey, prevention of soil drifting, tree planting, moving people from one section to another. Many, many millions

Supply-Agriculture

of dollars have been expended in the west to assist the growers of grain. We have had before us this year an appropriation of $35,000,000 to restrict the growing of wheat, or to bonus people for not growing wheat.
In eastern Canada we have rich areas of alluvial soil at the head of the bay of Fundy, as rich as any in all Canada, soil that attracted our earliest settlers, three hundred years ago. Such land had a selling value up to $150 and $200 an acre fifty years ago. It was the most attractive possession a man or woman could have as an investment. This property is to-day hardly worth owning except to those who are able to use it in their farming operations and who work it with their own labour. That is due to the reduction in the Value of the crops in relation to the cost of harvesting, the great reduction in yield and the quality of the crops.
The tides are up to sixty feet in. height at the head of the bay of Fundy. Many of the dykes built by pioneer settlers to protect these rich lands have broken down, and the lands are flooded. They have not been re-built because the owners of the property have not received returns of sufficient value to enable them to keep these dykes in repair. They have not been able to keep the canals open and ditch the marshes, with the result that tens of thousands of acres of our richest lands are becoming valueless. There are dykes broken down, aiboideaux washed away, water courses filled up, and large areas flooded. That is the condition in the east, at the head of the bay of Fundy in the constituency of the Minister of Finance, in Colchester, in Hants, in my own constituency of Cumberland, in Westmorland, in Albert county. If the government is spending $15,000,000 on farm rehabilitation and the construction of more than 31,000 water-control projects, irrigation works and so forth in the west, something should be done for eastern Canada, and there should be an appropriation to assist owners of marsh lands in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
I appeal to the minister and ask him if a small portion of the vote now before the committee could not be appropriated for assistance in controlling water, protecting and draining these very rich marsh lands at the head of the bay of Fundy in eastern Canada.
I am not objecting to what is being done for western Canad'a, but what the farmers and farm owners in eastern Canada have been receiving is not a drop in the bucket compared with the moneys that have been provided by parliament to assist owners of land and growers of grain in western Canada. [Mr. P. c. Black.)

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I would not wish to get into a discussion to-night on the amount of money spent east or west in connection with agriculture, but I have seen the dykes in the bay of Fundy, and I know they must have served a good purpose at one time. In some instances they still serve a good purpose, but there are others which I have seen in a state of disrepair which would make it necessary to do something about them. I do not know whether the responsibility lies here or elsewhere; I have not acquainted myself fully with the facts. I am informed that at least some of the money which was put into the construction of dykes in the early years was put up by the federal authorities. I have not looked into the facts in that regard, but I know there are many works along the streams and inlets in the eastern part of Canada upon which expenditure is being made, not by this department but by the Department of Public Works and other departments.
So far as expenditures in western Canada are concerned, they do not apply to all the west, but apply only to what is generally known as the drought area. Roughly speaking, a line is drawn about that dried-out area, and expenditures are made south of that line. For example, we do not make expenditures up in the Peace River country or in the northeastern part of Manitoba or in the extreme north of Saskatchewan. The line starts down in the neighbourhood of Winnipeg and runs in a northerly direction. It crosses the Alberta boundary where the Saskatchewan river crosses and then runs in a southerly direction to the Rocky mountains through Alberta. Therefore this is not an expenditure which is made throughout western Canada but is only in the area where the people have been suffering greatly from drought. As a matter of fact, 'it is made largely in the area which we did not throw open to settlement until after 1908.
Many of the lands in that area were used by the federal government until 1931 when they were turned back to the western provinces. During the regime of the previous government a commission was set up to investigate the matter, and it was reported at that time that somewhere in the neighbourhood of a figure which has been submitted to-night as having been spent on these
activities-$10,000,000, if I remember rightly___
was devoted to the purpose. The commission decided that about $6,000,000 is due to Saskatchewan and a similar amount to Alberta. Four million dollars has already been paid to Manitoba as a result of investigations made. These amounts were considered to be due to these sections because of the balance

Supply-Agriculture
between expenditures made by the federal government and amounts obtained by the federal government out of the sale of land and the disposal of land generally in the west. Consequently the balance is not all against the area in which these activities have taken place. Lands of the west were partly homesteaded, partly given to the railways to get them constructed across Canada, and sold in part to settlers who went in. That was not done in any other part of Canada. There is, therefore, in connection with the whole matter a problem involving many questions which I would not wikh to discuss under this item.
We have been doing something to assist in connection with soil surveys in the eastern provinces on much the same basis as we have done in the west.
In conjunction with the provincial department?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes, in cooperation with the provinces and the university staffs, by the making of grants. The other part of the work we have not done. We have not done it either in the east or in British Columbia or in the northern sections of the three western provinces. It is confined largely to what are known as the drought areas.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I wish to say a word in commendation of the subject matter raised by the hon. member for Cumberland. The locality to which he refer''' ' is not in my part of the province, but I spent five years in the immediate vicinity when I was going to school and am thoroughly familiar with it. In the last decade of last century, the nineties, there was no more prosperous part of eastern Canada, from the point of view of agriculture, than that part known as the Tantramar marshes. That statement is also true with respect to Grand Pre and other places in the counties of Kings and Annapolis in Nova Scotia. Their wealth was due to their productivity in hay and coarse grains. The lands have been protected over many years by these artificial barriers against the sea which were maintained under statutory authority by elected commissioners, I think in most instances under the control of the property owners themselves.
I well remember when I was going to school at Sackville marvelling at the number of carloads of beef cattle annually sent to the Halifax and Saint John markets from that community, many of them for the export trade to England. That has now to a large extent disappeared; just why, I have often wondered. I have made inquiry from landowners with regard to it, and they tell me that one of the 14873-227*
great blows to the prosperity of the country was the advent of the internal combustion engine, the loss of the market for the hay that came from the cultivated parts of those marshes, and the gradual loss of profit in the production of beef cattle. The result has been exactly as the hon. member for Cumberland stated.
We have in our community in the county of Sunbury and the county of Queens on the east side of the river St. John a comparable situation. We have the large plains of the St. John valley, the big alluvial deposits there and a large island section in the river. I remember that one of the first investments I ever made was in an island lot in the river St. John, from which I annually sold the standing grasses, and which fortunately for me I disposed of before the deluge came.
There is no doubt that there has been a great depreciation in the capital values of those lands nearly all of which were owned by the farmers. The minister has stated, mostly fairly I think, the situation of the west, and I sympathize with the condition he has delineated there. I am going to make a suggestion to the minister. Would he, and could he out of this vote or some vote in these estimates, send some scientific man or engineer to look over the whole position in the counties of Albert and Westmorland in New Brunswick and Kings, Cumberland, Annapolis and Colchester in Nova Scotia, with a view to establishing perhaps a policy in conjunction with the provinces-because I believe the provinces have an obligation also to do something to reestablish the fertility and wealth of a very large acreage of land which is unquestionably productive but which needs this protection from the sea water? It requires the rebuilding of dykes in certain places and drainage in and out of the sea. I do not think the amount of money required would be so very large The reason why it has not been done is the loss of profit from the product of these areas. Therefore the suggestion that occurs to me on the spur of the moment is that the minister's department interest themselves to the extent of sending a man this summer to make a survey of the whole position with a view to evolving some plan whereby the land would be reclaimed to a degree at all events, not only for the present owners but for future generations. I think something could be done. At all events, it would be a splendid gesture to the people of those counties. If the minister could see his way to divert even a few hundred dollars for a survey, then the whole situation could be considered at a later date. I am sure the
Sup-ply-Agriculture

hon. member for Cumberland, the hon. member for St. John-Albert, the minister who represents a very large area, and the hon. member for Colchester-Hants, would lend all the assistance they could in the way of showing the locality, perhaps driving the engineer round and interesting him in the problem, because it is a very real one.
All I would venture to ask of the minister to-night is that he take some money out of one of these votes and have a preliminary survey made. Then the whole problem could be considered and, if possible, some plan evolved which would save the situation. Time is, I think, somewhat of the essence. Unless something is done to protect these dykes, the whole country will sooner or later be inundated. I invite the minister to give his serious consideration, after the close of the session, to the suggestion I have made.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I think the former
government and, I am sure, the present government have guarded jealously the expenditure of this money as to the areas in which it is to be expended. It is most difficult even to propose getting outside that area, and I quite understand why that should be the situation. The federal government naturally did not wish to expend moneys on lands which are largely under the control of the provinces, apart from the areas where they felt some responsibility for having induced people to go in during a time when it was questionable whether it should have been settled.
I question whether we should or can do anything with this other problem. We have experimental farms at Fredericton and Nappan, and the staffs there worked along with the provincial authorities in making a survey of the very problem which has been raised here. We have had a committee working on it; a preliminary report has been made, and the report so far as it has been made would indicate that there are certain difficulties, which will be understood by both hon. members who have spoken. One of the difficulties is an economic one arising out of the change in conditions. The time when these marshes were giving the greatest returns was when cattle were being produced in much greater numbers than now. There are two problems: one, that of reconstructing and maintaining the dykes, and the other, that of what would be done with the land as against what was done with it in days when it was most profitable, namely, the growing of hay and grasses for cattle. Whether we can get back to that or develop some other kind of agriculture upon these lands is one question. I may be wrong 
in this. I have not discussed it with any of the authorities; I only say it because of what was said to me when I was there looking it over a few years ago. My understanding is that there is a condition in that soil which makes it peculiarly suited to growing certain kinds of grasses, and the fact that it has been flooded periodically over a long period of time by salt water has created a condition which requires a peculiar kind of cultivation in order to grow other crops than those grasses.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That, I
think, would apply only to a very much limited part.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
That is part of the
problem. All these matters are being surveyed, and reports are being made. To-night all I can say is that when we have a final report I think it will be found that the federal government and this department will sympathetically consider anything that can be done, and will assist as far as may be possible.

I do not wish to detain
the committee any longer than is necessary, but this work is being carried on under three or four distinct branches. For instance, there is water development and conservation, land utilization, community pastures and seeding down to permanent pastures, and soil drifting. Would the minister tell us briefly what, in his opinion, is the branch from which he is getting the best results in connection with the rehabilitation of western Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Of course they are all
related, and it would be difficult to name the one from which we are getting the greatest benefit. Water, in the form in which we are providing it, in most instances is only valuable if live stock can be maintained; and live stock can be maintained only if water and grass are available. Therefore the reseeding of land to grass is associated with the question of having water. Perhaps the work that has been done might be described in the shortest possible way by reading a letter I have before me I wrote to ask this lady for the privilege of using this letter on some occasion, and I do not know of any better time than right now, because I think it illustrates better than anything I could say the great benefit that is being obtained by our people on western farms from this work. I do not know this lady at all, but the letter is written by Mrs. George Calder, Junior, of Bow Island, Alberta,

Supply-Agriculture
addressed to Mr. Cavan, one of our officials, and it illustrates many of the things I have seen personally in the west:
Bow Island, Alberta,
October 29, 1940.
Dear Mr. Cavan:
I am writing to let you know how much my husband and myself appreciate the work of the PJ.EA.
Although we have been farming here for the past twelve years, this is the first year we have ever had a real garden. Thanks to the P.F.R.A. and its personnel whose assistance made this possible.
To those who live in areas where moisture is plentiful, a garden is taken as a matter of course, but to those of us in the drier areas who have struggled year after year only to see our garden dry out, to be able to grow a real garden and see it mature under the spell of plenty of moisture seems almost a miracle.
In spite of a constant fight against grasshoppers, we were able, by means of a small dug-out, a pump and an engine, to raise more than enough vegetables for our own use for the next year. I have canned over 125 quarts of beans, peas, corn, tomatoes and cauliflower, besides pickles galore. The _ cellar is full of potatoes, squash, beets, turnips, parsnips and citron. Besides, we had actually hundreds of watermelon and muskmelon. We had so many fresh vegetables during the summer that our grocery bill was $30 less than usual. The cash value of the garden for this year alone would be double the cost of construction, but to estimate the cash value of such a garden would cover only a small part of its real value. After seeing dried-out fields and lawns, to walk through or work in an oasis of thick green vegetables does something to one's morale and makes you feel as if life is worth living after all.
It gives one such a feeling of security to know that your cellar is full of vegetables, and every one knows that to maintain health we must eat vegetables. How much better to be able to grow them at home than to have to buy them in cans or depend on what the local store might have on hand!
We hope to be able to add fruits to our arden in another year. This will make the arm almost self-supporting, at a time when, due to the wheat situation, it may be needed most.
We sincerely hope that the dominion government will be able, in spite of the war, to carry on this wonderful work, so that many others will benefit as we have done.
Thanking you for your assistance, I remain, Yours very sincerely,
Viola E. Calder (Mrs. Geo. Calder, Jr.)
This letter describes better than I possibly could just what the construction of these dug-outs by the hundreds all over western Canada is doing not only for the economy of the west but also for the morale of the people; and, after all, I think the effect it has had on this woman, multiplied by a great number of families, is the most significant result we have had from the whole programme.
Did I understand the minister to say that the post office address of the writer of that letter was Bow Island, Alberta?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Yes.
Then do I understand that this farm is on an island in the Bow river?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No; Bow Island is not on or in any body of water. It is an inland post.
Then why is it called Bow Island?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am not just sure at the moment.
An island is something that is surrounded by water, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
A great many towns in western Canada have names that are hard to explain or understand. This may have been called an island because it is a dry
section of the country surrounded by different areas. If I may judge from this letter, that might be the situation.

I should like to add my voice to those who have spoken in commendation of the work which has been carried on under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, which I think is one of the most constructive measures that has been applied to western Canada in a long time. The work done in connection with soil surveys has been especi ally advantageous. In the early days of th; drought area many settlers moved volun tarily to the north, while others were moved by the government. Some of these settlers were placed on land which was not suitable for agricultural purposes. After a soil survey was carried out some years ago, many of these families had to be moved once more and placed on new blocks, the last of which was established some two or three years ago. When these people left the south they were assured by the government that they would be properly reestablished in the north. Therefore I should like to ask the minister if any part of this money is to be used to complete that reestablishment. I know some of the people have not been satisfactorily reestablished, and I have particular reference to one block south of the Canadian National line from Prince Albert to Hudson Bay junction. This block was established only two years ago, and as yet these people have not enough land under cultivation to be self-supporting.
Supply-Agriculture

I believe the government should do something to help to reestablish these families. Will any of this money be used for this purpose ?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No. Until this year we did have a fund, although not under this vote, which was used to help to take care of people who had been moved north. In 1932 the federal government undertook to pay one-third of the cost of moving a group of people from the southern parts of Saskatchewan and Alberta to the northern sections. I am not so familiar with what took place in Alberta; but, if I am not mistaken under this scheme about eight thousand people were moved to that area from the southern part of Saskatchewan. Many of those people got into difficulty, and we undertook to assist the provinces to take care of those people until they became sufficiently well established on the land to be able to take care of themselves. Since that time, the provinces have moved other people to that district, but that was entirely a provincial problem, and we did not spend any money to assist them. The fund which was in existence prior to last year has not been voted this year; the provinces are taking care of the problem themselves.

Yesterday I inquired
with regard to a proposed project on the Assiniboine river near Preeceville. I mentioned the fact that a great many dug-outs had been provided in northeastern Saskatchewan, which are very much appreciated by the farmers who are trying to get into mixed farming. What is the policy with regard to larger commitments in connection with projects such as the one on the Assiniboine? Is it proposed to complete that project this year, and what will be the cost?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There is a site at which the building of a dam would cost about $20,000. That is under consideration, but is not yet definitely passed. I believe it is in the vicinity of Kamsack. I would not be too sure about the exact location of it, but it is on the Assiniboine river. A number of dams have been under discussion, but the only one being considered for possible construction this year is one which would cost about $20,000.

I understand that the only benefit which would result from the construction of this dam would go to the town of Kamsack. I was wondering if this money could be used for the benefit of towns and cities; I understood that it was to be used for the rehabilitation of agricultural areas. I know that the town of Kamsack is short of

water, and that the building of this dam would help. I do not, however, believe that it would benefit any farmer in that area.

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
There are two dams listed here. I believe neither of them is in the mind of the hon. member. One is in the vicinity of Canora, on the White Sand river, and the other is in the vicinity of Preeceville. The engineer's description of the Preeceville dam is that it consists of storage works to be constructed on the Assiniboine river a short distance above the town of Preeceville, for the purpose of storing flood water in lakes Lomond and Annie Laurie-both Scotch. This water would be released at low-flow periods for domestic stock watering and for irrigation purposes for farmers in communities located adjacent to the Assiniboine river valley between Preeceville and Brandon,
The intention of building there is not just that of helping the town, although it may have that effect. The main object is, however, to provide water during the summer months in greater volume by storing it in the spring. At one time the headlands of the Assiniboine were clothed with poplar trees which held the snow in the spring. The intention of this kind of work is to bring about a similar effect by the artificial storage of water in lakes, and permitting it to go down during the summer months, thus avoiding a rush in the early spring. That is the intention; it is not that of helping any particular town, but rather of helping many areas all the way along.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
SO. Special. Prairie Farm Assistance Act, $500,000.

To-day we had presented to us an amendment in connection with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. There is no act, the administration of which causes members representing rural constituencies more trouble than does this one. That arises because the administration of the act, in so far as the regulations are concerned, has departed from its intention. There are also certain anomalies in connection with the administration of the act which I should like to bring to the attention of the committee, and particularly to the attention of the minister, so that, if he sees fit so to do, he will cause the act to be amended accordingly.
In the first place let me point out that under the act "farmer" is defined as a person engaged in farming in the spring Wheat area.

make a suggestion? There are only three items left in the estimates for my department. It would appear that the discussion of this item may take some time, and we have only a few minutes left. the time of the committee, as someone has suggested.

speechtext:
Then I move that this
item be allowed to stand.

We were advised
that the bill would be proceeded with this afternoon. I have waited here throughout the evening for this item to come up. But now that there is an opportunity to discuss it-

I am not suggesting

How will this money
be spent, and in what provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: It may be spent in any province of Canada, but it will be spent in order to improve cheese factories, and since most of the cheese factories are located in Ontario and Quebec, a greater part of this will be spent in those two provinces. It will be spent to encourage the building of new cheese factories?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No; it is spent for consolidation, where it is desired to bring two or more cheese factories under one construction in order to eliminate the number of factories and bring about more efficient production. It is not for the building of entirely new factories.
What percentage approximately of the cheese factories in Ontario have been equipped with modern refrigeration plants?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: There have been fifty-four assisted this year, and I understand that there are about 600 cheese factories in Ontario. It was about the same number the year before. It varies from year to year.
Then I take it that the greater number of cheese factories are not equipped with modern refrigeration plants?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Some may have been equipped before this policy was introduced. Our intention was to encourage factories to put in equipment to produce the type of cheese form which they desire to have in Britain. Another reason was that we wished

to encourage the putting in of storage equipment which would keep the cheese in good shape. Those two activities have been carried on in the different factories. Some had the equipment before, and others we have assisted.

I should like to know what position a cheese company is in which had already got equipment and received a bonus from the department, then lost its building and outfit by fire. Will it be reimbursed? Will it get a subsidy towards a new building?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The way that has been handled to date is that they get half of the difference between the cost of reconstruction and the insurance they collect as a result of the fire.
What is the reason for the increase of a quarter million dollars in this item?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: This includes premiums as well as what we have been discussing, the improvements in factories. There is a premium of one cent on cheese that scores 93 and two cents on cheese scoring 94. The amount of cheese which gets into these two grades is increasing year by year, and, in addition, there is an increased quantity of cheese manufactured. Cheese production has risen since this policy was started, from 120,000,000 pounds to 140,000,000 pounds, and we hope it will be higher this year.
Does this vote take care of the extra cent which the minister announced the other day?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No; that comes under war measures.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
32. Special. To provide for assistance for the replacement of maple production equipment, $75,000.
Where will this be spent?

speakerposition: Minister of National War Services; Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It will be spent in the province of Quebec. We had an agreement with them prior to the war under which we were to spend $300,000 a year, the Quebec government a similar amount, and those who had the equipment undertook to spend a similar amount to change over from the equipment used for making maple sugar and maple syrup. Lead poisoning got into the maple sugar and maple syrup from the equipment which had been used. It had a lead cover on it to prevent rust, and the Americans were refusing to take this product unless we undertook to change the equipment. Accordingly we made this agreement with the Quebec

The War
government, we paying one-third, they paying one-third, and the persons interested, one-third. This year they did not wish to spend the amount that we were providing, and we cut it down to $75,000.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Progress reported.

Friday, June 6, 1941.
